Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guideline C62Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry Methods provides guidance for the development and verification of liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) methods in the clinical laboratory. The document is intended to reduce interlaboratory variance for clinical assays through guidance for evaluating interferences, assay performance, and other pertinent characteristics. It emphasizes particular areas related to assay development and presents a standardized approach for method verification that is specific to mass spectrometry (MS) technology. This document is intended for laboratorians responsible for development and verification of MS-based assays, physicians who may use these assays for patient care decisions, external quality assessment programs, and manufacturers of MS instrumentation and reagent kits designed to be paired with a particular mass spectrometer. This document is limited to discussion of LC-MS and is focused on the steps for development of a method, eg, whether the analyte is a drug, hormone, protein, or peptide.
Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI). Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry Methods. 2nd ed. CLSI guideline C62 (ISBN 978-1-68440-154-3 [Print]; ISBN 978-1-68440-155-0 [Electronic]). Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, USA, 2022.

chunks.text:
The importance of mass spectrometry (MS) in the clinical laboratory is increasing, and this CLSI document was developed in response to the need for increased robustness and harmonization of liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LCMS) methods. Vendors of in vitro diagnostic devices often wait until the clinical utility of a particular assay is established and widely accepted before beginning development of a commercial assay. As a result, improvements in patient care can be delayed until a commercial assay is available. These delays can be significant if there are difficulties in the development of the assay. For laboratories with the capability to develop and implement laboratory-developed tests, MS provides an attractive alternative solution based on the ability to rapidly develop an analytically robust assay with excellent analytical sensitivity and specificity. In some cases, it offers an attractive alternative to commercially available assays that have already been developed, but do not offer acceptable performance in the current clinical context. LC-MS technology shows promise as a tool to rapidly develop clinical assays for emerging biomarkers coming from research in proteomics. Advances in instrumentation are likely to enable application of LC-MS technology in routine clinical diagnostic testing.
Despite the significant advantages that can be gained from incorporating MS into the clinical laboratory, considerable challenges exist. Among these is the fact that for some assays, significant laboratory-to-laboratory variability for the same analyte has been observed. There is currently limited assay standardization for MS-based methods, and much of the assay variability can be attributed to the lack of commercially available calibrators; that is, each clinical laboratory must formulate its own calibrators. For example, some sites may use powdered or commercially lyophilized material, some may use organic solvent solutions, and some may even use formulations obtained from their institution's pharmacy to make calibrators. Moreover, the preparation of the calibrators also varies from using solutions made in buffer, from using analyte-free serum or plasma as the matrix, or from using patient specimen remnants as the calibrator matrix-a problem for endogenous analytes. Differences in chromatographic methods from site to site lead to variable matrix effects during analysis. In addition, many laboratories verify their assays using various protocols in accordance with different regulatory or industry standards. This document addresses these issues by providing guidance for the development and verification of LC-MS methods in the clinical laboratory.

chunks.text:
This document outlines many important elements for successful implementation of LC-MS technology for clinical analyses. The basic instrument components needed both for chromatography and MS are discussed, along with instrument parameters that must be optimized for development of robust LC-MS methods. In addition, the document contains a discussion of preexamination considerations that must be addressed during the method development process. Various elements of method development are summarized, along with best practice recommendations for addressing those elements during the process. Guidance is provided for verification of an LC-MS method, including a recommendation for preverification evaluation before full method verification. Finally, the document provides guidance for QA, including assay QC and postimplementation monitoring.

This document outlines many important elements for successful implementation of LC-MS technology for clinical analyses. The basic instrument components needed both for chromatography and MS are discussed, along with instrument parameters that must be optimized for development of robust LC-MS methods. In addition, the document contains a discussion of preexamination considerations that must be addressed during the method development process. Various elements of method development are summarized, along with best practice recommendations for addressing those elements during the process. Guidance is provided for verification of an LC-MS method, including a recommendation for preverification evaluation before full method verification. Finally, the document provides guidance for QA, including assay QC and postimplementation monitoring.

This document provides an introduction to, and guidance for, method development, verification, and postimplementation monitoring of quantitative clinical applications using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). While LC-MS may also be used for qualitative analyses, the focus of this document is on the use of this technology for quantification of clinical analytes. In addition, while there are commercial and research methods that allow direct injection without chromatography for rapid analyses, this guideline is exclusively focused on liquid chromatography (LC) coupled to mass spectrometry (MS). The purpose of this guideline is to educate both clinical LC-MS practitioners and health care providers (including physicians) who may use these assays for patient care decisions on the benefits and limitations of LC-MS methods used in the clinical laboratory, as well as provide a practical guide for the development and implementation of LC-MS-based clinical applications. It is intended to serve not only as a companion to CLSI document C50,  which serves as 1 excellent general guidance for MS in the clinical laboratory, but also to provide an enhanced focus on methods, best practices, and instrumentation related to LC-MS, which is emerging as the most common approach to clinical analyses. This document is also intended to be a resource for instrument manufacturers, manufacturers of LC-MS reagents, regulatory agencies, and educators, as well as individuals responsible for developing laboratory standards and policy.
A description of all current clinical applications of LC-MS, as well as all of the pertinent information regarding development and verification of these methods, is beyond the scope of this document. As such, this guideline directs the reader to appropriate existing resources wherever possible. In providing guidance for LC-MS method development, verification, and implementation, this document focuses on:
· Important features of LC-MS instrumentation
· Preexamination factors that can impact assay performance and utility
· Assay calibration
· Analytical variables important in method development
· Assay verification
· QA and QC
· Postimplementation monitoring of clinical methods

Because it is often impossible to know what isolates or specimens might be infectious, all patient and laboratory specimens are treated as infectious and handled according to 'standard precautions.' Standard precautions are guidelines that combine the major features of 'universal precautions and body substance isolation' practices. Standard precautions cover the transmission of all known infectious agents and thus are more comprehensive than universal precautions, which are intended to apply only to transmission of bloodborne pathogens. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) address this topic in published guidelines that address the daily operations of diagnostic medicine in human and animal medicine while encouraging a culture of safety in the laboratory.  For specific precautions for preventing the laboratory transmission of all known infectious agents 2 from laboratory instruments and materials and for recommendations for the management of exposure to all known infectious diseases, refer to CLSI document M29. 3

chunks.text: CLSI, as a global leader in standardization, is firmly committed to achieving global harmonization wherever possible. Harmonization is a process of recognizing, understanding, and explaining differences while taking steps to achieve worldwide uniformity. CLSI recognizes that medical conventions in the global metrological community have evolved differently in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere; that these differences are reflected in CLSI, International Organization for Standardization (ISO), and European Committee for Standardization (CEN) documents; and that legally required use of terms, regional usage, and different consensus timelines are all important considerations in the harmonization process. In light of this, CLSI's consensus process for development and revision of standards and guidelines focuses on harmonization of terms to facilitate the global application of standards and guidelines.

In order to align the usage of terminology in this document with that of ISO, the term accuracy , in its metrological sense, refers to the closeness of the agreement between the result of a (single) measurement and a true value of a measurand, and comprises both random and systematic effects. Trueness is used in this document when referring to the 'closeness of agreement between the expectation of a test result or a measurement result and a true value'; the measurement of trueness is usually expressed in terms of bias Precision . is defined as the 'closeness of agreement between independent test/measurement results obtained under stipulated conditions. As such, it cannot have a numerical value, but may be determined qualitatively as high, medium, or low. For its numerical expression, the term imprecision is used, which is the 'dispersion of independent results of measurements obtained under specified conditions.' In addition, different components of precision are defined in C62, primarily repeatability , ie, 'the closeness of the agreement between results of successive measurements of the same measurand carried out under the same conditions of measurement; while ' Reproducibility describes the closeness of agreement of results of measurements under changed conditions. Measuring interval has replaced reportable range when referring to 'a set of values of quantities of the same kind that can be measured by a given measuring instrument or measuring system with specified instrumental uncertainty, under defined conditions.' An interval [ a b ; ] is delineated by two limits, a and b b ( > a ), whereas a range (r[ a b ; ]) is expressed as the difference between b and a b ( -a ). Thus, the range of the interval [ a b ; ] is the difference ( b -a ) that is denoted by r[ a b ; ]. Similarly, the term analytical measuring interval has replaced analytical measuring range .
The term measurand is used when referring to the quantity intended to be measured instead of analyte (component represented in the name of a measurable quantity); the term measurement procedure replaces analytical method for a detailed description of a measurement according to one or more measurement principles and to a given measurement method, based on a measurement model and including any calculation to obtain a measurement result.
Verification focuses on whether specifications of a measurement procedure can be achieved, whereas validation verifies that the procedure is fit for purpose. Both concepts can describe procedures of varying complexity.

trueness - the closeness of agreement between the expectation of a test result or a measurement result and a true value (ISO 3534-2) ; 7 NOTE: Trueness is usually expressed numerically by the statistical measure bias that is inversely related to trueness. See also accuracy and bias.
upper limit of the measuring interval (ULMI) - the highest measurand concentration at which all defined performance characteristics of the measurement procedure are met.
validation - confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled (ISO 9000) 12 ; NOTE 1: The World Health Organization defines validation as 'the action (or process) of proving that a procedure, process, system, equipment, or method used works as expected and achieves the intended result' (WHO-BS/95.1793) 13 ; NOTE 2: The components of validation are quality control, proficiency testing, validation of employee competency, instrument calibration, and correlation with clinical findings.
verification - confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled (ISO 9000) 12 ; NOTE: A one-time process completed to determine or confirm test performance characteristics before the test system is used for patient testing.

chunks.text: LC is a technique used to separate analytes of interest in a mixture based on their differential equilibrium between a stationary phase (solid or liquid immobilized on a solid support contained in a column) and a mobile phase (solvent/solvent mixture that flows through the column). The use of a pump to deliver mobile phase at a constant flow rate by applying pressure and injecting the sample onto the chromatographic column while maintaining an uninterrupted flow of solvent at a positive pressure results in a technique known as highperformance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Based on its compatibility with automation and its characteristic reproducibility, HPLC has gained popularity among analytical chemists and is the LC technique of choice for LC-MS applications. There are several variations in HPLC technique that are used along with MS, including nanoflow HPLC and ultra-high performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC), which offer some advantages over traditional HPLC, including increased separation efficiency, greater resolution, and shorter analysis times.

chunks.text:
The essential hardware components of modern HPLC systems used for clinical LC-MS methods typically include mobile phase reservoirs, mobile phase degassers, mobile phase pumps, mixers, an autosampler system, a temperature-controlled column oven, and a flow control system. Additional features include automated rack changers and switching valves.
The autosampler introduces the sample into the HPLC system flow path. Use of a temperature-controlled autosampler with insulated sample racks should be considered in order to maintain optimum sample stability. There are a variety of autosampler configurations available, virtually all of which are suitable for LC-MS-based assays. A 'needle-and-loop injector' is characterized by an autosampler needle that draws a specified volume of sample from a vial and places the sample into an 'off-line' sample loop, which is then switched 'in-line' such that the mobile phase flows through the loop. The sample is then moved to the head of the column. Then, the autosampler needle is taken 'off-line' and washed before the next injection to reduce the risk of sample carryover. A 'flow-through injector' design also draws the sample into a needle, but the needle then becomes a part of the solvent flow path, constantly passing solvent through the needle and then to the head of the column. The exterior of the flow-through needle is washed before the next sample injection.

chunks.text:
The HPLC pumps provide accurate and reproducible flow rates of mobile phase and sample through the system. Binary pumps have two solvent inlet lines and can blend two solvents for isocratic or binary gradient elution procedures. A quaternary pump has four solvent inlet lines, which can accommodate complex chromatographic separations that require up to four mobile phase components. In addition, quaternary pumps can allow concurrent use of multiple methods with multiple mobile phase combinations. Accurate and precise mobile phase pumps are required for reproducible retention times and peak areas (or heights); therefore, pump quality should be investigated before purchase. HPLC system pressure requirements depend on column packing size, column length, and column internal diameter. Standard HPLC pumps can accommodate pressures of 5000 to 6000 psi (approximately 34 000 to 41 000 kPa, or 345 to 415 bar) while ultra-high pressure pumps can accommodate pressures in excess of 19 000 psi (approximately 131 000 kPa, or 1310 bar). Pumps and mixers should be rated for the desired pressure requirements. Plastic polymer tubing is chemically resistant, easy to manipulate, and is generally sufficient for standard HPLC pressure applications. Stainless steel tubing is required for high-pressure systems. Pressure requirements must also be considered when selecting frits, ferrules, and unions.
To improve the reproducibility of retention time and peak height/area, dissolved gases should be removed from the mobile phases. Manual or inline degassing of mobile phases after preparation or mixing is advisable. Most modern HPLC systems contain integrated vacuum degasser systems to remove small amounts of dissolved gases from the mobile phases that may adversely affect chromatography.

chunks.text: HPLC switching valves increase the flexibility and throughput of the system by allowing use of multiple columns (multiplexing) or the application of different gradients to one or more columns (eg, on-line solid phase extraction [SPE] or two-dimensional chromatography). Multiplexing systems increase sample throughput by allowing analysis from two, four, or more columns with eluates directed to a single mass spectrometer. Elution of the analyte is slightly offset in time for each column in order to take advantage of mass spectrometer analysis speed. It should be noted that multiplexing systems require additional hardware components such as extra pumps, degassers, and valves. Addition of a switching valve after the column allows diversion of a select portion of the eluate to the mass spectrometer, with the remaining eluate going to waste. These types of postcolumn switching valves help keep the mass spectrometer clean and are highly recommended if sample preparation does not remove all matrix components.

chunks.text:
One key element of the stationary phase is the size of the particles. Initially, stationary phases had a particle size of about 40 µm. HPLC columns with a particle size of 10 µm were introduced in the 1970s, and later, in the 1990s, columns having particle sizes as low as 2 µm became available. Columns having particles less than 2 µm are now available for more efficient separations. Stationary phase supports having small particle sizes (< 2.0 µm) can achieve separation using shorter columns with smaller diameters, as compared to longer columns that were previously required for high resolution. The use of small particle sizes in combination with shorter and narrower columns, at the operating pressure of standard HPLC systems, can lead to shorter retention times and the serious side effect of extra-column band broadening. 14 Although the use of small particle sizes typically results in improved peak resolution, HPLC system pressure increases as particle size decreases. Standard HPLC pumps have maximum pressures of 5000 to 6000 psi (approximately 34 000 to 41 000 kPa, or 345 to 415 bar). Recently, several HPLC vendors have designed systems that can operate successfully at higher pressures (> 10 000 psi [approximately 69 000 kPa, or 690 bar]), thus taking advantage of the improved resolution accomplished by using small particle sizes. Hence, the use of these systems is more appropriately referred to as 'ultra-high' performance LC.
By using ultra-high pressure systems, column particle size can be reduced and separation times shortened for complex mixtures without losing resolution (ie, the peaks are narrower). Use of UHPLC systems also allows increased flow rate, which enables shorter run times with high throughput of samples. When choosing between HPLC and UHPLC systems, one has to consider factors such as difficulty involved in the separation of analytes in complex mixtures, daily testing volume, method development required, and cost.

There are a variety of ion sources available for mass spectrometers. Some of these ion sources are 'direct ionization sources,' in which analytes are directly ionized from a surface or from a solution. Atmospheric pressure ionization sources, which are discussed in this chapter, produce ions from analytes in solution and are more commonly used in clinical assays. There are a number of texts that treat ion sources in greater detail. 15,16 Also, for more detailed descriptions about ion sources commonly used in clinical MS, see CLSI document C50. 1 For the purposes of this document, only three ionization sources will be considered:
· Electrospray ionization (ESI)
· Atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI)
· Atmospheric pressure photoionization (APPI)
These sources are summarized in Chapters 4.2.1, 4.2.2, and 4.2.3, respectively, as well as in Table 1.

chunks.text: ESI is perhaps the most commonly used ionization technique in clinical MS. It is a very sensitive ionization technique for analytes that exist as ions in the LC solvent. A solvent spray is formed by the application of a high voltage potential held between a stainless steel capillary and the instrument orifice, and by the axial flow of a nebulizing gas (typically nitrogen). Solvent droplets from the spray evaporate in the ion source of the mass spectrometer, releasing ions to the gas phase for analysis in the mass spectrometer. Although ESI is a very sensitive ionization technique, it is also subject to matrix effects, particularly ion suppression. When using ESI, care should be taken to evaluate, reduce, and monitor ion suppression (see Chapter 6.7.2).

4.2.1 Electrospray Ionization

Solvent droplets from the spray evaporate in the ion source of the mass spectrometer, releasing ions to the gas phase for analysis in the mass spectrometer. chunks.text: APCI uses heat and a nebulization gas to form an aerosol of the eluent from an LC system. In contrast to ESI, a strong voltage potential between the capillary needle and instrument orifice is not used to ionize the analyte of interest. Instead, a corona discharge is used to ionize solvent molecules and analytes in the aerosol. Ions released to the gas phase are then analyzed by the mass spectrometer. During ionization in the APCI source, some thermal degradation may occur, which results in a greater degree of fragmentation in electrospray ionization. For the best analytical performance using APCI, source ions should be heat stable and volatile. APCI may be less susceptible to matrix effects (including ion suppression) as compared to ESI, and may be considered for many applications, including measurement of nonpolar analytes.

chunks.text:
APPI is an alternative, though less frequently used, mechanism to ionize analytes eluting from a chromatography system. The solvent is first vaporized in the presence of a nebulizing gas (eg, nitrogen) and then enters the instrument ion source at atmospheric pressure. There, the mixture of remaining solvent and analyte molecules is exposed to a UV light source that emits photons having an energy level that is high enough to ionize the target molecules, but not high enough to ionize air and other unwanted molecules. A dopant (commonly toluene) is often used to increase ionization efficiency.

ESI, Principal Benefit(s) = • Sensitive ionization technique for polar analytes • Broad applicability in clinical MS • Multiply charged ions, which allow for analysis of larger molecules (ie, > 1000 Da). ESI, Principal Limitation(s) = Maybemoresensitive to matrix effects as compared to APCI. APCI, Principal Benefit(s) = • Typically less sensitive to matrix effects than ESI • Mayprovide better sensitivity for less polar analytes. APCI, Principal Limitation(s) = • Typically only singly charged ions are formed, limiting the effective mass range, ie, unsuitable for proteins, peptides, and other large molecules • Maybeunsuitable for thermally labile analytes. APPI, Principal Benefit(s) = Works well with nonpolar analytes and has potential to ionize analytes that do not ionize by either ESI or APCI.. chunks.text: When coupled to an HPLC/UHPLC system, the mass spectrometer functions as an ion detector. The analyte of interest is ionized in the source of the mass spectrometer by any of a variety of mechanisms (see Chapter 4.2). Once ionized, analyte ions travel to the mass analyzer component of the mass spectrometer, where ions are selected according to their mass-to-charge ratio ( m/z ). Ions produced from small molecule analytes (< 1000 Da) usually possess a single charge; therefore, their m/z is equivalent to the mass of the ion. This is commonly designated as [M + H] +  for protonated (positive) and [M - H]  for deprotonated (negative) ions. -The selected ions then travel to the detector where they are counted. The data output is presented as a mass spectrum, with the m/z plotted on the x-axis and the relative abundance of ions plotted on the y-axis. When coupled to an LC system, a chromatogram can be generated in which relative ion abundance of a specific m/z is plotted vs time (see CLSI document C50 1 ).

headings: 4.3 Mass Analyzers: Quadrupole, Time-of-Flight, and Ion Traps

chunks.text:
A quadrupole is a set of four conducting rods arranged in parallel, with a space in the middle. The rods are electrically connected to each other in opposite pairs. Quadrupole mass analyzers separate ions based on the stability of their flight trajectories through an oscillating electric field in the quadrupole. The field is generated when a radio frequency (RF) voltage is applied between one pair of opposing rods within the quadrupole. A direct current voltage is then applied in addition to the RF voltage. Only ions of a certain m/z will have a stable flight path through the quadrupole; other ions will have unstable trajectories and will not reach the detector. The RF and direct current voltages can be fixed in a way that the quadrupole acts as a mass filter or analyte-specific detector for ions of a particular m/z . Alternatively, the analyst can scan for a range of m/z values by continuously varying the applied voltages.
Single quadrupole mass spectrometers contain a single mass analyzer and can only measure ions formed in the instrument source, whether they are intact molecular ions or fragment ions formed by in-source fragmentation. Therefore, single quadrupole mass spectrometers do not generally provide a large amount of structural information and specificity is limited when compared to tandem quadrupole mass spectrometers.

chunks.text: A tandem quadrupole (sometimes known as a triple quadrupole) mass spectrometer contains two quadrupole mass analyzers separated by a collision cell. Precursor ions are selected by the first quadrupole mass analyzer. The selected precursor ion(s) is then fragmented in the collision cell by a process known as collision-induced dissociation (CID). CID results from collisions of the analyte of interest with an inert gas, such as nitrogen or argon. The structure of the specific product ions produced by CID is a function of the bond energies inherent in the molecular structure of the precursor ion. Product ion patterns and relative ion abundance can be highly reproducible if the CID conditions are maintained in a consistent manner. Specific product ions are selected by the final quadrupole mass analyzer and are passed to the detector. A precursor/product ion pair is called a mass transition. Thus, only analyte ions having a specified mass transition (precursor/product ion pair) are able to reach the detector, resulting in the high specificity of tandem quadrupole mass spectrometric methods. This mode of data acquisition is referred to as selected reaction monitoring (SRM). When multiple transitions are monitored, the approach can also be called multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). Use of SRM improves sensitivity and signal reproducibility because the instrument spends all available time monitoring only the transitions of interest. By using SRM, accurate and precise quantitation of target analytes can be achieved (see CLSI document C50 1 ).

chunks.text: Time-of-flight (TOF) mass analyzers separate ions by virtue of their different flight times over a defined (fixed) distance. Ions are accelerated (pulsed) into a flight tube such that ions of like charge have equal kinetic energy. Because kinetic energy is equal to 1/2 mv , where 2 m is the mass of the ion and v is the ion velocity, the lower the ion's mass, the greater the velocity and shorter its flight time. The travel time from the source of the ion pulse through the flight tube to the detector can be transformed to the m/z value through the relationship described above. All ion masses are measured for each ion pulse. Thus, TOF mass spectrometers offer high sensitivity and a high duty cycle. Historically, TOF mass spectrometers have been used for qualitative experiments in which high resolving power and exact mass measurements are necessary (eg, metabolite identification and protein sequencing). However, modern TOF mass spectrometers are capable of accurate and precise quantitative measurements. Although tandem quadrupole mass spectrometers should still be considered the instrument of choice for small molecule quantitative clinical MS, TOF mass spectrometers are gaining acceptance for such analyses (see CLSI document C50 1 ).

chunks.text: Ion trap mass analyzers exist in three different geometries: 1) 3D, or Paul ion traps; 2) linear ion traps; and 3) electrostatic ion traps. Mass spectrometers that include an ion trap analyzer are most commonly used for qualitative work (eg, metabolite identification, protein identification, and screening applications). Many other instrument configurations are now available that combine two or more mass analyzers of different design, and are therefore called 'hybrid instruments.' One such hybrid combines quadrupole and TOF mass analyzers. In this instrument, the quadrupole mass analyzer performs precursor ion selection, while a TOF mass analyzer performs the product ion analysis. Another hybrid combines a quadrupole with a linear ion trap; this instrument has found a niche in toxicology screening for unknown agents (see CLSI document C50 1 ).
A greater diversity of mass spectrometers exists than is covered in this chapter. The choice of mass spectrometer depends on its intended use. Although tandem quadrupole mass spectrometers are by far the most common type of mass spectrometer used in the clinical laboratory, the use of others should not necessarily be excluded. 17 Care should be taken when selecting an appropriate LC-MS system for the laboratory. Method sensitivity, throughput, and robustness requirements, as well as system cost, are all factors that must be balanced when evaluating systems for purchase. Numerous mass spectrometer models are available today from a variety of vendors, and they may vary substantially in terms of analytical sensitivity and quality. Acquisition of the highest quality instrumentation (within the laboratory's budget constraints) may reduce method performance limitations and result in fewer instrument problems. Other factors to consider include:
· Software (eg, ease of use)
· Terms of warranty
· Cost of subsequent years of service contracts
· Availability of technical support
· The purchase of a new vs refurbished instrument

The temperature of the LC column is a key parameter that affects retention time, peak shape, resolution, column efficiency, and, to a lesser degree, analyte sensitivity. Use of higher column temperatures (50 to 70°C) may provide performance advantages such as decreased peak width, increased separation efficiency, and decreased retention time. 18-20
Higher temperatures also reduce the viscosity of the mobile phase, resulting in decreased LC system pressure. Therefore, increasing column temperature is one way to accommodate higher flow rates without loss of peak resolution or efficiency. It should be noted that temperatures that are too high may impair analyte interaction with the column or cause degradation of the stationary phase, or the analyte itself. LC column temperature should be optimized during method development.
CLSI eCLIPSE - Taylor Pobran - VCH/PHC Labs - Vancouver Coastal Health/Providence Heal... - 10/31/2022. Unauthorized duplication or network sharing is not allowed.
Variability in the temperature of the column may result in irreproducible retention times, decreased peak resolution, and peak broadening. 18 Therefore, column temperature must be controlled. Column temperature may be maintained through tight control of the room temperature or by wrapping the column in an insulating material. However, the most accurate method to maintain temperature is the use of mobile phase heaters or placement of the column in a temperature-controlled column oven. 19
Heating of the mobile phase inside the tubing can improve peak shape and avoid peak broadening due to thermal variation between the tubing and the column. 19 Mobile phase temperature stability may be achieved by placing mixers, valves, and tubing inside the column oven, or a mobile phase precolumn heater may be purchased. Many of today's commercially available LC systems can be purchased with active solvent preheating capabilities.

chunks.text: Sample injection volume affects method sensitivity, peak shape, and peak resolution. Increased sample injection volume is one way to increase method sensitivity; however, care should be taken to avoid overloading the column. Column overloading may result from either excess sample volume or solute concentration that exceeds the binding capacity of the column. Broad peaks, peak fronting, or peak tailing may be observed if the column is overloaded. 21 Fused-core columns, or use of narrow bore columns with reduced packing, can be susceptible to column overloading problems. In addition, it is important to note that increasing sample volume may not result in the desired increase in sensitivity because injecting larger volumes often increases the background noise. Concentration of the injected sample can correct volume overload, while dilution of the sample or use of a column with increased capacity may be required under conditions of excess solute. Care should be taken to ensure that the solvent composition of the injection solvent is closely matched to the initial mobile phase conditions. If a mismatch in solvents occurs, solute precipitation may occur, leading to system blockage and/or premature wear of system components.

Mass spectrometers are capable of analyzing both positive and negative ions. Typically, acidic compounds will form negative ions and basic compounds will tend to form positive ions. During assay development, the instrument polarity can be hypothesized based on the functional groups of the analyte (or from published sources). However, it should not be assumed that all analytes will behave in the same manner on all mass spectrometers. Thus, the instrument polarity should be selected based on empirical evidence. Some analytes will
form both positive and negative ions. The choice of instrument polarity then lies with the mode of operation that produces acceptable sensitivity and reproducibility.
Modern tandem quadrupole mass spectrometers allow for rapid switching between monitoring positive and negative ions; thus, both acidic and basic compounds may be monitored in a single experiment. The manufacturer's guide should be consulted for minimum polarity switch times because these may be greater than the interchannel delay time within a single polarity analysis. Interchannel delay time is discussed in more detail in Chapter 4.4.2.11.

chunks.text: One parameter that may significantly affect analyte signal (and S/N ratio) in an electrospray ion source is the capillary voltage. Capillary voltage, typically measured in thousands of volts (kilovolts, or kV), is required to help form the solvent spray from the tip of an electrospray probe. Ranges for the capillary voltage are typically 1 to 5 kV. Varying the capillary voltage in the presence of an infusion of a constant amount of the analyte of interest will allow for a preliminary determination of the optimum setting. Additional experiments may be required to optimize system sensitivity in the presence of matrix. Thus, on-column injections of an extracted sample should be made, and the capillary voltage modulated, until the highest S/N ratio is obtained. Once an optimum capillary voltage is selected, it rarely needs to be changed during routine instrument operation. If the capillary voltage needs to be adjusted in order to restore system sensitivity, the capillary may require cleaning or replacement.

chunks.text: The desolvation gas aids in the evaporation of solvents and liberation of ions into the gas phase. Desolvation gas (often nitrogen or air) is passed over a heating element and then is directed at the spray emanating from the tip of the probe. In some instrument configurations, there is a coaxial flow of desolvation gas that encompasses the electrospray probe tip. Optimizing the desolvation gas flow and temperature will improve the sensitivity of an assay and help to maintain a robust system. In general, the higher the LC flow rate and the higher the percent aqueous composition of the mobile phase, the higher the desolvation gas flow rate and temperature required.

chunks.text: Typically, quadrupole mass spectrometers operate at unit mass resolution (0.7 atomic mass unit [amu] by the full width half maximum [FWHM] definition). For small molecule quantitation, a mass resolution of 0.7 to 1 amu FWHM for the first quadrupole mass analyzer is common. Due to the selection of precursor ions in the first quadrupole mass analyzer, the second quadrupole mass analyzer may be set to a more open (lower) resolution (eg, 1 to 1.5 amu FWHM) in order to increase assay sensitivity. Recently, the benefits of higher resolution quadrupole mass analyzers, particularly in the first quadrupole, have become available. By increasing the mass resolution of MS1 to 0.2 to 0.5 amu FWHM, the background signal may be reduced. However, care is needed when operating in these elevated resolution modes because environmental factors (eg, temperature and humidity) may adversely affect an assay. For a detailed description of mass resolution, see CLSI document C50. 1

chunks.text: Dwell time refers to the amount of time (in milliseconds) that the instrument collects signal for a specified m/z or SRM transition. Sensitivity and precision of quantitation may be improved by increasing the dwell time, but doing this may reduce the number of different transitions that can be monitored in a single assay. The best practice recommendation is that dwell times should be optimized so that 15 to 20 data points are collected across a chromatographic peak; 10 is the minimum amount for good peak characterization. 23  Staggered time windows for detection of ions and transitions may also be used to increase the instrument's duty cycle.

4.4.2.11 Interchannel Delay Time
Interchannel delay time is the time (in milliseconds) between individual SRM transitions. This delay time is required to clear ions from one mass transition from the collision cell before ions from the next mass transition enter the collision cell. This will avoid product ion cross-talk. Product ion cross-talk is discussed in further detail in Chapter 6.5.2.

Ion detectors for mass spectrometers are manufactured in various configurations. The detector is typically comprised of a semiconductive material, held at high potential, that releases electrons when ions strike the detector. In an electron multiplier-based detector, electron signal is then amplified and converted into a digital signal. In a photomultiplier-based detector, electrons strike a phosphor screen that releases photons of light. The light is then amplified by a photomultiplier tube. As with all analytical systems, the response of the detector will degrade over time. The detector 'gain' may be manipulated (according to manufacturer instructions) to increase signal intensity by compensating for normal degradation of response over time. However, the need for excessive adjustment of response may indicate replacement of the detector is required. Detector degradation is more pronounced with electron multiplier-based systems than with photomultiplier-based systems.

By definition, exogenous compounds are those not produced in vivo , but introduced from an ex vivo source; sometimes it can be difficult to differentiate, especially with steroids. The primary means of introducing exogenous substances into the body include inhalation, gastrointestinal absorption, intravenous injection, and skin absorption. There are different categories of exogenous substances, including therapeutic drugs, drugs of abuse, supplements, topical ointments, and environmental substances. In order to determine the appropriate specimen type and sample collection time for laboratory monitoring, it is critical to know the pharmacokinetics of an exogenous substance.
Sample types for consideration are blood, serum or plasma, urine, saliva, and hair; however, whole blood, serum, plasma, and urine are the most common specimen types. For example, if drugs are strongly bound to RBCs (eg, cyclosporine A, tacrolimus, sirolimus), whole blood is needed for analysis, while for other drugs (eg, antiepilepsy drugs, antipsychotic drugs, mycophenolic acid) either serum or plasma is preferred. Urine is a preferred specimen type for many applications in toxicology due to the ease of sample collection and the enrichment of drugs and metabolites in urine. Oral fluid concentrations of many drugs correlate with the blood-free drug concentrations, while hair can be used to assess chronic exposure. However, these specimen types are not widely used as routine clinical specimens.

chunks.text: For therapeutic drug monitoring and toxicology testing, in which the blood concentration is correlated with drug dose, therapeutic, and/or toxic effects, a quantitative analysis is required. Depending on the specific pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationship for the drug, trough (or predose) concentrations are monitored, while for other substances, peak (or postdose) concentrations are better clinical indicators. For many drugs (eg, busulfan), multiple time points are collected to determine the drug exposure (ie, area under the curve) and dosing strategy. Depending on the metabolic pathways, kinetics, and in vivo metabolite activity for each drug, parent forms of some drugs (eg, cyclosporine A, tacrolimus, sirolimus) are more important, while metabolites are more important for others (eg, mycophenolic mofetil, oxcarbazepine, cocaine). As a result, understanding the metabolism of each drug and the pharmacokinetics of the metabolites is important.

Development of an LC-MS assay for endogenous analyte measurement will benefit from knowledge of the primary biological pathway that uses the molecule (biomarker). The biological effects monitored through surrogate measurement of the biomarker will include either up or down regulation (or both) in order to assess a related enzymatic or cofactor abnormality. As such, additional endogenous species that are upregulated should be reviewed for possible isobaric interferences in MS-based testing. 24,25
Factors associated with regulation of endogenous analytes are critical to the clinical utility of measurement and the timing of specimen collection. Examples of rhythmic variations include measurement of hormones as a function of monthly cycles (eg, progesterone in menstrual cycles) or circadian rhythm (eg, melatonin and cortisol diurnal variations). Knowledge of these variations should be addressed as limitations to patient sample collection (eg, date and/or time of draw) and appropriate reference intervals generated based on these constraints. Furthermore, circulating concentrations of certain endogenous analytes (eg, reproductive hormones) vary as a function of a patient's sex and the stage of maturation. The use of age and sex-appropriate measurement ranges may need to be considered due to drastic changes in circulating concentrations during prepuberty, Tanner stages in puberty, and pre-, peri-, and postmenopause. 25

chunks.text: The sample collection process of venipuncture represents an analytical variable for consideration in endogenous analyte measurement. The experience of venipuncture can induce stress and may facilitate overproduction of stress-related hormones and their respective catabolic products, such as corticotrophin-releasing hormone, vasopressin, cortisol, and catecholamines. 26 Undergoing a change from supine (lying down) to standing, or vice versa, yields nonspecific variations in blood concentrations due to a dynamic fluid shift, which results in a change in plasma volume (reduced when standing, increased when supine) and the subsequent alteration of nondiffusible molecular constituents. These nonspecific variations may be on the order of 4% to 15% and may take 10 to 30 minutes before reaching stasis. 27 Additionally, certain analytes are directly affected by posture, such as catecholamines, and plasma renin and aldosterone, requiring specific procedures for sample draw or posturespecific reference intervals. 28,29 These sample collection variables should be carefully controlled, both when determining reference intervals and when performing patient testing.

Endogenous and exogenous small molecule analytes very rarely exist freely in plasma. In some cases, specific high-affinity binding sites are inherent in human biology. In other cases, nonspecific binding sites of moderate affinity are abundantly available. Regardless of the stoichiometry and affinity of each binding site, the apparent concentration and equilibrium of bound and unbound analyte can significantly affect the efficiency of extraction from a patient specimen. As a result, normal physiological processes that alter specific binding site concentrations (eg, pregnancy, malnutrition) need to be investigated for their influence on extraction efficiency. Hyperproteinemia due to other physiological processes (eg, severe dehydration, monoclonal gammopathy), should also be investigated as a potential source of interference. Other potential causes of altered binding-site concentrations include increased RBC fragility, traumatic blood draws, and diminished kidney or liver function.
It is well known that lipids can interfere with ionization and are easily copurified with analytes of interest. In addition, analytes may partition preferentially in the neutral lipid core or phospholipid monolayer of lipoprotein particles in plasma. It is therefore important to identify the influence of lipid/lipoprotein concentrations (eg, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides) on extraction efficiency, and the potential interference of postprandial alterations in lipid profiles should be evaluated. Patients with recognized disorders of lipid metabolism can be excellent sources of samples for interference studies (eg, familial hypercholesterolemia, familial combined hyperlipidemia, severe chronic kidney disease). Experiments to fully characterize assay interferences are described in Chapter 7.4.

chunks.text: Lastly, isobaric compounds or isobars (compounds of the same precursor mass that share a fragment mass with the analyte of interest) can similarly interfere with both endogenous and exogenous analytes. During the development of a specific chromatographic-mass spectrometric program, interference from known abundant endogenous isobars should be avoided as much as possible (see Chapters 6.7.1 and 7.4). The primary method for avoiding interference from isobars is through improved chromatographic resolution (see Chapter 6.4.2). However, many administered drugs or their metabolites can be isobaric with the analyte of interest, and changes in metabolism in the patient can lead to increases in low-abundance molecules. Several databases exist that can be searched for isobaric compounds and the exogenous compounds identified. Physiological influences on the concentrations of endogenous analytes should be carefully considered for potential preexamination interference. A compendium of databases of potential interferences which can be searched by monoisotopic mass has been established by the National Institutes of Health (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih. gov/pccompound). A smaller, and potentially more relevant, database of drugs and metabolites has also been established (http://www.drugbank.ca).

During the last decade, plastic blood collection tubes have been gradually replacing glass tubes. Plastic tubes are not only less expensive, but also safer than glass tubes because they are less likely to break. Replacement of glass tubes for plastic tubes is a particularly important issue for many endocrine assays, especially peptide hormones. These analytes often degrade rapidly and can adsorb to a variety of surfaces. Changing from glass to plastic tubes can also be problematic for analytes that are regarded as stable. An example of the latter can be seen in therapeutic drug monitoring, where plastic tubes have been shown to influence the measured concentrations or stabilities of several drugs. Similar concerns may apply to low molecular weight hormones, such as steroid hormones and biogenic amines. It is conceivable that low molecular weight organic substances released by plastic tubes could interfere in some of these assays and that small changes that are not detected by immunoassays would change the results of more specific methods. Finally, in certain situations, such as serial monitoring of tumor markers, even minor discrepancies between glass and plastic tubes may gain significance during changeover from one type of collection vessel to the other. 30
Both plasma and serum are aqueous solutions (about 95% water) containing a variety of substances, including proteins and peptides. The primary difference between the two sample types relates to the molecules involved in the clotting process. The clotting of blood maximally stimulates eicosanoid (prostaglandins, prostacyclins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes) biosynthesis, and, thus, serum concentrations of these metabolites do not reflect physiological concentrations. In addition, matrix effects manifested in certain tests may require the use of only serum or only plasma as a sample type. It has been demonstrated that matrix effects can be avoided if the same brand of plastic tubes for processing and storing plasma samples and spiked plasma standards are selected. 31 It is important not to assume that serum and plasma results for a particular analyte will be equivalent. If a laboratory wishes to accept both sample types (serum and plasma), then testing must be performed in order to evaluate whether the results are comparable, or whether or not a separate calibration is required for each matrix. This must be conducted for each method for which more than one sample type is accepted.

chunks.text: Serum- and plasma-separator tubes contain polymeric gels with several constituents to adjust specimen viscosity, density, and other physical properties. Rubber stoppers and the plastics comprising tube walls may shed polymeric components or plasticizers. Previous studies have reported effects of blood collection tubes on a variety of laboratory tests. Although the potential effects of blood collection tubes need to be considered for any laboratory test, this may be particularly important for MS-based laboratory tests, which measure a broad spectrum of different components in a single analysis. 31

The addition of an IS into samples before analysis represents the single most valuable method enhancement that MS offers over other detection techniques. The IS is used to account for recovery variance and matrix effects. It must have a number of key attributes for success, namely, an IS should be unique to the test system and be a physicochemical mimic for the analyte being measured. Due to the milieu of possible extraction losses, as well as LC separation variance and ionization effects that occur in LC-MS assays, it is highly recommended that all quantitative LC-MS assays use methods that include use of IS. IS should have the following properties:
· The IS should be unique in the testing population (ie, it should not be an endogenous or commonly dosed compound).
· The IS should not coelute with interferences having the same mass transition as compounds from the testing population (including possible drug metabolites).
· The IS should have similar physiochemical properties to the analyte being measured.
· The IS should have similar chromatographic retention time to the analyte being measured.
· The IS should be added into samples at a concentration that does not interfere with analyte lower limit of the measuring interval (LLMI) measurement through intrinsic impurities or contribution of unlabeled compound (in the case of isotopic labeling).
· The IS should be added at a reproducibly measurable concentration into samples (eg, 10 to 50 times LLMI).
· The IS should be added in a miscible solution to samples, particularly when endogenous binding proteins are present.

chunks.text: IS selected for use in an assay may also be structurally similar, such as those used in LC-UV methods, but not identical (eg, an additional methyl group in an acyl side chain for an exogenous drug moiety). Such a compound is considered an analog for the analyte being measured. Certain analog moieties should be avoided (eg, hydroxylation), which are easily fragmented from the molecule during ionization, thus generating the compound of measure. 32 Where multiple steps are involved in samples preparation/analysis, analog IS may not control for bias (trueness and/or imprecision). The failure of analog internal standardization to control for bias is almost exclusively related to physicochemical differences. This results in differences in analyte binding, extraction, chromatographic elution, and ionization efficiency for assays in which the properties (described above) have been controlled through appropriate assay design. Additionally, analog IS should be strenuously validated and closely monitored during sample analysis. Reviews of consistency in analog IS response should be performed with each batch, particularly if IS do not exhibit all of the characteristics listed above.

chunks.text: It is strongly recommended that the IS for mass spectrometric assays is a stable isotope-labeled form of the test analyte. By definition, a stable isotope is a nonradioactive isotope and is the preferred enrichment due to stability (avoiding degradation) of IS to unlabeled test analyte and safety of nonradioactive isotopes. As such, it is not recommended that isotopes such as iodine-125, tritium, or carbon-14 be used in LC-MS assays. The majority of commercially available stable labeled IS incorporate enrichment with deuterium ( H or D), carbon-13 2 ( 13 C), nitrogen-15 ( 15 N), oxygen-18 ( 18 O), or combinations thereof. Appropriately selected stable labeled IS can meet all requirements of the properties listed above because they can perfectly mimic the test analyte and be independently measured by the mass spectrometer due to mass difference generated through isotopic enrichment. 33 In some instances, the position of deuterium atoms can lead to hydrogen-deuterium exchange in a mass spectrometer interface or in the gas phase, resulting in variability for IS response and, in extreme cases, complete loss of deuterium atoms. 34 Furthermore, when many deuterium atoms are incorporated into a stable label, the physicochemical properties are no longer consistent with the test analyte, often observed through subtle differences between LC retention time between analyte and IS. 35,36 In these eventualities, it may be desirable to select an alternate labeling strategy incorporating chemical stability, such as 13 C and  15 N. These chemically stable forms of IS are preferred when commercially available.

The degree of labeling should be such that interference from naturally occurring isotopes in the target analyte at the upper limit of the measuring interval (ULMI) is less than 5% of the IS response. This can be assessed by predicting or measuring the isotope cluster for the analyte and determining the relative intensities of the isotope-rich peaks that would overlap with those of the IS. As a general rule, for molecules of less than 1000 amu, a + 3 amu isotopic enrichment should suffice for analytes, which do not contain atoms with significantly different naturally occurring isotopic abundances, such as chlorine ( 35 Cl and 37 Cl) and bromine ( 79 Br and 81 Br). Changes in the degree or location of labeling (a new IS) must be verified before use. In tandem MS using collision-induced dissociation, the fragment ions used to generate quantitative data from analyte and IS should represent similar fragmentation pathways. Ideally, the fragment ions generated by the IS should contain at least some of the
heavy isotopes from the enriched parent. However, this is not always feasible in practice. It is also important to note that no labeling is ever 100% complete. The amount of IS used should be such that the concentration of unlabeled material in the IS does not significantly interfere with the quantitation.

chunks.text: Internal standardization may be used in two discrete modes in LC-MS assays. Commonly, the IS are used as a normalization control (isotope dilution assays) and absolute chemical and isotopic purity are not generally required. In this mode, IS solutions are added to all calibrators, QC materials, and test samples at a fixed concentration. Isotopically labeled IS should contribute < 20% of the test analyte LLMI response. 37 Assay calibration is performed through generation of a plot of analyte to IS peak area ratios (y-axis) vs known concentrations of test analyte (x-axis). Concentrations of QC and test specimens are assayed against the calibration plot through a back-calculated measurement of their analyte/IS area ratio. The second mode uses the IS to generate signal for response/dose calibration, often at a single concentration. This method requires that the concentration and purity of the IS be known. The ionization properties of the IS must be identical to the test analyte or, at a minimum, the relative bias between them must be thoroughly described and known. It may be appropriate to add the IS at a medical decision point of the test analyte, thereby performing a ratio of analyte peak area to IS peak area, and multiplying the ratio by the added concentration of IS to quantify the analyte concentration. The majority of LC-MS assays use the first method of isotope dilution. It must be stressed that the second method of isotope dilution is an approach that needs robust verification across the proposed measurement range in many different patient samples.

One of the primary benefits of using MS for clinical laboratory applications is the ability to achieve a high degree of analyte sensitivity (LLMI). Many systems can measure analyte concentrations in the pg/mL range, or even lower. However, the ability to achieve high sensitivity also results in substantial susceptibility to interferences due to impurities found in reagents and consumables. Even small amounts of impurities may affect specific mass transitions or may influence broad mass transition ranges. The presence of impurities may result in interfering peaks or a high background signal for one or more mass transitions.
Impurities may arise during the formulation of a reagent or the manufacture of a consumable. There have been reports of interfering peaks or high background noise due to leaching of impurities from specific brands of consumables used for sample preparation, such as specimen collection tubes, plastic pipette tips, microcentrifuge tubes, and microtiter plates. Significant interfering peaks have been observed for certain testosterone methods due to contaminants from common serum-separator tubes used for specimen collection. 38  Assay interference has been reported when using a particular brand of polypropylene microcentrifuge tube for a 25-hydroxyvitamin D method. 39 In addition, some laboratories have found that use of HPLC-grade deionized water as a mobile phase component results in high background signal for a broad range of transitions, while use of MS-grade deionized water does not exhibit the interference. It is therefore critical that the laboratory use the highest purity reagents and highest quality consumables possible.
Careful selection and verification of solvents used for LC-MS analysis is important because impurities found in solvents can cause ion suppression. Increased temperatures may decrease stability of analytes and other reagents, which can compromise the concentration or purity of the analyte. Therefore, all reagents must be stored correctly and according to manufacturer specifications. Hygroscopic compounds must be kept dry for accurate weight measurements during reagent preparation. Reagents and solvents should be capped tightly during storage to prevent evaporation. Increased temperatures may decrease stability of analytes and other reagents which can compromise the concentration or purity of the analyte.

Manufacturers of reagents and consumables may vary the processes used in the manufacturing process, or may use different source materials to produce the products. Therefore, interferences due to impurities may suddenly appear when a reagent or consumable lot or vendor is changed. The effect of impurities is frequently method or instrument specific, and may be observed using one manufacturer's method or mass spectrometer and not another's, even if the same mass transitions are monitored. Interferences can also be introduced by processes within the laboratory. For example, contamination from improperly washed glassware or use of common equipment such as degassers or nitrogen evaporators may introduce impurities into the reagents or samples.
Whenever possible, MS-grade solvents and deionized water should be used to prepare reagents. However, HPLCgrade solvents may be used if lack of impurities can be demonstrated for multiple solvent lots. The laboratory should evaluate the purity of all reagents and confirm the absence of interferences from consumables and collection tubes during the initial method verification process. If interference is detected, the laboratory can analyze each reagent and consumable separately until the product that is contributing the impurity is identified. If interfering peaks are present in an extracted neat solvent sample, the most likely source is from one of the reagents and the exact cause would require further investigation to determine which one. More detailed information on evaluation of interferences can be found in Chapter 7.4.
The standard operating procedure (SOP) should specify the vendor and catalog number for all reagents and products used in the method. All lot changes of solvents, extraction reagents, columns, filters, and other components of reagents and consumables (pipette tips, tubes, microtiter plates, autosampler vials, etc.) must be documented. Certificates of analysis (COAs) for each reagent or consumable lot must be maintained, when available. New columns and HPLC tubing should be washed and equilibrated before use to remove residual impurities from the manufacturing process.

Certain analytes exhibit molecular changes due to light exposure; thus, SOPs should clearly document experimental conditions under which to perform assays in order to prevent such occurrences, particularly when the control of these conditions is critical to the final results (eg, UV-protected glassware, yellow lighting). Adsorption of analytes to containment vessels should also be obviated or controlled during sample analysis, even when employing isotope dilution methods. Certain chemical processes used in LC-MS assays, such as derivatization of target compounds or liquid-liquid partitioning, often require specific procedural control (eg, time of derivatization, temperature control, vessel). Total allowable batch size may also need to be constrained
due to the implicit scale of preparative wet chemistry required to execute these steps appropriately. Changes in environmental conditions due to temperature (eg, samples being left on the benchtop following extraction before placement in the autosampler) should be documented in the SOP with tolerances or maximum proven storage noted.
For many methods, a sample preparation step will be required before LC-MS analysis. For some methods, this step may be as simple as a protein precipitation by adding an organic reagent to a blood sample 42 ; or in some cases, it can be a complex, multistep derivatization or digestion and extraction procedure. 43 Other common specimen pretreatments include SPE, supported liquid extraction, and liquid-liquid extraction. It is not the purpose of this document to discuss all of the various approaches to specimen preparation; however, it is important to consider the variables associated with the necessary preparation steps for the analysis, as they may impact the analyte stability or the design of the method during development. In addition, the verification of the method must account for the entire process, including the specimen preparation before LC-MS analysis.

The most common modes of acquiring MS data are:
· Full scan acquisition, which results in a total ion chromatogram (TIC)
· Selected ion monitoring (SIM)
· SRM (or MRM)
A TIC provides a representative plot of the total ion current over the course of the chromatographic run; however, it is not specific for a particular compound, and has little to no utility for quantitative analyses. SIM is a nonscanning MS technique that may be used for quantitation of specific analytes. In SIM, the mass spectrometer is set to scan over a very small mass range. Only compounds with the selected mass are detected and plotted. The SIM plot is a more specific plot than the full scan TIC plot. However, SIM falls short in its lack of specificity, especially when the resolution is only to nominal mass, and the analysis is performed in very complex matrixes, such as blood. 44

chunks.text: SRM, like SIM, is a nonscanning MS technique. In SRM, both of the mass analyzers are used as mass filters to monitor a particular fragment ion of a selected precursor ion. For example, in tandem quadrupole MS, the first (quadrupole 1 [Q1]) and last (quadrupole 3 [Q3]) mass analyzers are used as mass filters to isolate a precursor ion and its corresponding product ion or ions. The signal of the product ion is then monitored over the chromatographic elution time (see Figure 1). The specific pair of m/z values associated with the precursor and product ions is referred to as a 'transition' and can be written as (precursor [ m/z ])/(product [ m/z ]) (eg, 684.5/556.3). Unlike SIM, no mass spectrum is recorded in an SRM analysis. Instead, the detector acts as a counting device for the ions matching the selected transition, thereby returning an intensity value over time. The combination of the specific precursor mass and its unique product ion is used to selectively monitor for the compound to be quantified. As this is a very selective analysis mode, SRM can increase S/N ratio, which in turn increases the analytical sensitivity of an assay. When choosing a precursor or product ion, it is strongly recommended to avoid use of a loss of 18 mass, representing a loss of water molecule, which can be nonspecific in many settings. Additionally, if derivatization is used during sample preparation, use of a precursor or product ion that represents loss of the derivative should be avoided.

chunks.text: Multiple SRM transitions can be measured (MRM) within the same experiment on the chromatographic time scale by rapidly selecting between the different precursor/product ion pairs. Typically, a tandem MS instrument cycles through a series of transitions and records the signal of each transition as a function of the elution time. The method allows for additional selectivity by monitoring the chromatographic coelution of multiple transitions for a given analyte 45 (see CLSI document C50 1 ). However, although this capability allows for a multianalyte assay using a single chromatographic run, one should remember that as more transitions are monitored at any given time (eg, when monitoring multiple analytes in one injection), fewer data points across a peak are collected, and the data may be less reliable if an insufficient number of data points are available to characterize a chromatographic peak area measurement (see Chapter 6.4.5). Monitoring multiple transitions for a single analyte also yields increased specificity for an assay by allowing monitoring of a qualifier ion in addition to having an ion used for quantitation. Additional guidance for use of a qualifier ion is given in Chapter 9.2.5.

1. Prepare a solution of the analyte of interest at a concentration recommended by the manufacturer.
· If the solution is too dilute, signal may not be observed. If the concentration is too high, the instrument may be contaminated.
· Prepare the solution with some proportion of organic solvent to effect desolvation.
· The solution should contain a low concentration of proton donor, proton acceptor, or appropriate adduct-containing component, eg, 0.1% formic acid or ammonium hydroxide.

5. Apply collision gas to quadrupole two and determine product ions by observing Q3 spectra.

· Using a t-union, connect a length of tubing from LC pumps to syringe pump tubing.
· Set up LC pumps to flow at elution conditions as described above and concurrently infuse analyte with syringe pump.
· Manually or automatically optimize source conditions, ie, desolvation gas flow rates and temperatures, source voltage, and probe position (if applicable), to effect optimum analyte signal.

After direct infusions of the analyte of interest have been carried out, the user should have identified at least two SRM transitions for each analyte:
1. A quantifier transition, which is typically the most selective transition and is used for quantitation of the analyte
2. A qualifier transition, which serves to confirm the identity of the analyte, thereby enhancing the selectivity of the measurement
Using the area of the chromatographic peak for the quantifier and qualifier transitions, it is possible to calculate the ion ratio for each analyte and IS.
Once the SRM transitions are optimized for the assay, they should not be changed after development is complete and assay validation has been started. Changes after the beginning of assay validation will require the validation to begin again. From this point of assay development forward, the ion ratio for each analyte should be recorded and monitored in order to determine the expected variation in this measurement, such that a mean deviation and SD can be calculated. There should be very little variation in this calculated ion ratio as long as the ionization conditions remain constant. Variation is indicative of an interference in the assay 47-49 (see CLSI document C50 1 ).

chunks.text: There is a wide of array of stationary phase chemistries commercially available today in a variety of particle sizes and column dimensions. Some of these chemistries are used for highly specialized applications (eg, separation of chiral compounds), and some (notably reverse phase hydrophobic interaction columns, eg, C4, C8, C18, phenyl, phenyl-hexyl) have broader applicability to clinical LC-MS. In these latter columns, the stationary phase or 'bonded phase' is chemically bonded to a supporting material such as spherical silica or polymeric materials. The combined material is then packed into a cylindrical column in a uniform manner to create an HPLC or UHPLC column. The choice of stationary phase will depend on the analyte(s) of interest. The choice of column is generally based on the chemical composition for the analyte of interest, but a literature search will almost always reveal a stationary phase that may be suitable for a particular analyte.

6.2.1 Stationary Phase Chemistry
There is a wide of array of stationary phase chemistries commercially available today in a variety of particle sizes and column dimensions. Some of these chemistries are used for highly specialized applications (eg, separation of chiral compounds), and some (notably reverse phase hydrophobic interaction columns, eg, C4, C8, C18, phenyl, phenyl-hexyl) have broader applicability to clinical LC-MS. In these latter columns, the stationary phase or 'bonded phase' is chemically bonded to a supporting material such as spherical silica or polymeric materials. The combined material is then packed into a cylindrical column in a uniform manner to create an HPLC or UHPLC column. The choice of stationary phase will depend on the analyte(s) of interest. The choice of column is generally based on the chemical composition for the analyte of interest, but a literature search will almost always reveal a stationary phase that may be suitable for a particular analyte.

chunks.text:
The quality of the stationary phase is largely beyond the control of today's clinical chemist. HPLC and UHPLC columns are available from a number of reputable manufacturers and these manufacturers will often share information about their QA procedures, and many provide a COA with each individual column. The COA, if provided, will typically demonstrate individual column characteristics (eg, US Pharmacopeia tailing, pressure, retention time, and retention factor). A representative chromatogram may also be included. The COA may also provide information about the batch of stationary phase used to pack the column (eg, particle consistency, pore structure, impurity analysis, carbon content, and surface coverage of the bonded phase). All results must pass the manufacturer's acceptability criteria before the column is released for distribution.
When changing columns, it is important to check the retention time, peak height, peak width, and resolution of the new column using a system suitability sample (SSS) (see Chapter 9.2.1). It is not unusual for the retention time of an individual compound to change from one column lot to the next and this change, if present, will need to be accounted for in the MS methods and quantitation methods. However, variability in the other column chromatography parameters may indicate a problem with the quality of the new column.

The term 'mobile phase' refers to the solvent(s) used to move analytes through the HPLC column. It is typically made up of one or more solvents coupled with additives such as acids, buffers, and ion-pairing reagents. Most quantitative LC-MS analyses are done with reversed phase (RP) chromatography in which the mobile phase is more polar (water/organic) and the stationary phase is less polar (alkyl bonded). Separation in the RP is affected by many parameters of the mobile phase such as percentage of the strong solvent, type of solvents, ionic strength of the mobile phase, pH of the mobile phase, and the additives added to the mobile phase. Some common suitable solvents for LC-MS analysis are water, acetonitrile, methanol, ethanol, acetone, and tetrahydrofuran.
In RP chromatography, water is usually used as the weaker (more polar) solvent, which is referred to as solvent A and is used along with a stronger (more nonpolar) solvent referred to as solvent B. For this chromatographic approach, a high percentage of strong solvent may be used to elute almost all components off quickly. If increased resolution of compounds is required, then the percentage of strong solvent should be decreased. When there is a significant period of time between areas of resolution in a chromatographic separation, using a gradient

chunks.text: The general criteria for selecting solvents and additives are volatility, moderate ionic strength, and appropriate pH for ionization. Types of additives to be avoided are nonvolatile salts (which lead to frequent cleaning and poor signal), inorganic acids like hydrochloric acid (which are corrosive and affect the LC-MS interface) and surface active agents (which suppress ESI). When using additives like buffers to alter pH, their solubility must be taken into account. It is important to note that ion-pairing agents can suppress the signal in MS. Instead of using ionpairing agents for better chromatography, it is generally preferred to identify a column chemistry that is more suited for the compound(s) of interest. Alternately, a very low concentration (< 0.02%) of ion-pairing agent may be used, which may not affect ionization.

Separation of an analyte from interfering substances may be accomplished by isocratic or gradient elution, and the choice of elution type significantly impacts chromatographic separation. Maintaining a constant mobile phase composition (constant percentage of the two or more solvents mixed together) during the course of the chromatography is known as isocratic separation or elution. For new method development, users often start with isocratic conditions, as it is a simple approach to chromatography. However, although isocratic elution may allow for simpler chromatographic methods, late-eluting compounds exhibit peak spreading, and peak shape deteriorates with repeated sample injections.
Conversely, in gradient elution, the composition of the mobile phase is varied over the course of the run. For RP methods, the percent of aqueous mobile phase typically starts relatively high and the percentage of organic solvent is gradually increased. Compared to isocratic elution, gradient elution requires a longer equilibration time between samples, but may provide increased analyte selectivity (resolution of matrix components from the analyte), superior run-to-run retention time stability, and more reproducible peak shapes. Gradient elution generally extends the column lifetime and is more consistent than isocratic elution when a column does need to be replaced. Modern advances in pump technology have significantly reduced variation in mobile phase mixing during gradient elution. 50,51
