In any new method development by RP LC, whether using isocratic separation or gradient separation, the following steps must be followed in order to fine tune the mobile phase. 52 The user must select the proper choice of organic solvent, followed by adjusting the percentage of solvent B to obtain an optimum capacity factor (k ) ' of two to 10. In addition, the user should check for tailing of peaks and, if present, this should be eliminated by varying one (or a combination) of the following:
· pH and buffer concentration
· Percentage of solvent B
· Temperature
· Organic solvent choice
Adjusting the pH is crucial for separation of ionizable analytes and in gradient separation. Additionally, trimming gradient range and altering the gradient slope may be required when performing a gradient separation.

When preparing mobile phase, it is recommended to use high-purity (preferably MS-grade [minimum UHPLCgrade]) and particle-free solvents and reagents. 53 HPLC-grade or MS-grade prefiltered solvents are commercially available from many manufacturers. When buying a solvent, if it is not specified as prefiltered with a 0.2-µm (or smaller) filter, check with the manufacturer to confirm that the solvent was prefiltered with a 0.2-µm (or smaller) filter. UHPLC-grade water, which is particle free, chemically clean, and with 18-megohm-cm resistivity, should be used when using water as the solvent. This will reduce the amount of impurities in the water that can collect on the column during equilibration with the weak solvent. The purification process should include all of the following steps:
· Reverse osmosis (to remove most contaminants)
· UV sterilization (to kill bacteria)
· Ion exchange (to remove any remaining ions)
· Carbon filtration (to remove any remaining organics)
· A pharmaceutical-grade 0.2-µm membrane filter (to remove any remaining particulates)

chunks.text: The mobile phase reservoir should be an inert container. It should be covered to prevent dust from entering, and vented to prevent a partial vacuum from forming. Brown glass bottles of appropriate size (based on flow rate and length of the run) should be used. Use of an inlet-line frit (sinker frit) is required to keep the inlet at the bottom of the reservoir and to remove large particles. Excessive air in the mobile phase can be avoided by degassing of the solvent before use. It is important to have an expiration date for the mobile phase and to check the quality of the mobile phase on a regular basis. When changing mobile phase, avoid 'topping off.' Instead, discard the old solvent, rinse the bottles and solvent inlet filters with the solvent that will be used, and refill the bottle with fresh solvent. Finally, perform a wet prime of the column. Any glass container used to prepare or store mobile phase must be thoroughly cleaned (rinsed with organic solvent, then with water, and finally with the solvent that will be put into it) before use. Glassware used to prepare or store mobile phase should be stored separately from other common-use glassware.

In order to achieve a very stable retention time, the LC system must be operating properly and factors such as temperature, mobile phase composition, and column conditions must be highly controlled and described in appropriate detail in the method SOP. This practice ensures that constant retention times are produced for both the analyte and the IS. Once an LC-MS method has been optimized, it is important for the retention time to remain constant for accurate peak selection for analysis and quantitation of samples. In fact, the variation should remain within ± 2.5% of the retention time between runs (see CLSI document C50 1 ). Factors that can affect the retention time of an analyte include the LC mobile phase solvents, pumps, and column.
The preparation of the mobile phases used for LC-MS analysis can greatly affect the retention time. For example, in RP chromatography, there is an exponential relationship between the percentage of organic solvent present in the mobile phase and retention time of the analyte. Additionally, it is advisable for the mobile phases to be premixed before introduction to the column, in order to ensure proper mixing, and also to prevent temperature fluctuations that may occur when solvents are added to water. If modifiers are added to the LC mobile phase solutions, control of the pH and concentration of the buffers should be carefully monitored; a slight shift in pH may result in a retention time shift for the analyte of interest. The working condition of the LC pumps is also important to the retention time. Shifts in retention time may be observed if inaccurate flow rate and mixing of the mobile phase solvents occur due to pump malfunction. Steps should be taken to ensure that equipment is operational and preventive maintenance plans are in place. Another important factor that affects retention time is temperature. The temperature of the solvents, samples, and the column can cause fluctuations for isocratic separations. This can be minimized with the use of a column thermostat during analysis.
The proper time or number of column volume equivalents (five to 10) needed to equilibrate a column should be used after each run; otherwise, a shift in retention time may be observed. Additionally, a change in retention time may be the result of increasing back pressure in the column, guard column, or frit, indicating changes in flow of the mobile phase. In addition, oversaturation of the column by the analyte and sample integrity should be considered when troubleshooting retention time alterations.

The resolution ('Rs' in the equation below) of two chromatographic peaks A and B is a measure of separation of these compounds and is defined as the distance between the two peak centers, divided by average peak width.
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->
where t  is the retention time and w is the width of each peak (see Figure 2). r
Figure 2. Chromatographic Resolution of Components A and B (Used with permission from the University of Chicago Clinical Chemistry Laboratories.)
In general, complete baseline resolution is achieved with Rs of at least 1.25. For any given value of Rs, the separation of components becomes more ambiguous when one of the two peaks is much smaller than the other. Peak resolution and, therefore, compound separation varies with three independent factors 54 that should be optimized for every clinical method:
1. Separation factor (alpha). This factor includes column and/or mobile phase selectivity and composition. General approaches to improving compound separation, ranked in order of decreasing effectiveness are:
· Change of mobile phase composition
· Change of mobile phase pH
-  This step is restricted to ion-exchange chromatography, in which ionized species are separated.
· Change of stationary phase
-  Changing the column type is not as convenient as mobile phase modifications because a new stationary phase will likely require further modifications of mobile phase composition.
· Change of temperature
-  Although resolution of some compounds (eg, cyclosporine A) improves with temperature, it should be noted that an increase in temperature leads to a decrease in solvent strength.
2. Column efficiency. This parameter has traditionally been modified by increasing the column length and/or column pressure (ie, the flow rate) and decreasing particle size. Today, however, the small-particle columns are routinely used in LC and are already optimized by the manufacturer to provide maximum column efficiency.
3. Mobile phase composition. Mobile phase usually consists of an optimal mixture of two solvents with different strengths (eg, organic and aqueous solvent). In general, the larger the aqueous component, the weaker the solvent strength and longer the separation times. If the solvent is too strong, however, the components will be poorly resolved. It is important to determine and maintain optimal solvent strength while any of the individual separation factors are modified.

chunks.text: As mentioned, each of the three parameters listed above is fairly independent and can be optimized independently. In determining the resolution needed for a given separation, one should always keep in mind that the prediction of experimental conditions is only an approximation and that the column performance degrades over time, leading to a decrease in Rs. Therefore, a margin of safety with overestimation of Rs is generally desirable when new LC method parameters are established. While resolution between analytes is generally desirable for chromatography-based assays, it is important to remember that with LC-MS, multiple transitions can be monitored within the same chromatographic peak, so baseline resolution of analytes is not absolutely necessary. Often in LC-MS methods, a pragmatic balance is struck between speed of analysis and chromatographic resolution.

Use of guard columns between the injector and the column to remove unwanted matrix components (such as proteins and lipids) before separating analytes of interest from biological matrixes is common practice. The proper selection of guard columns and analytical columns is a key consideration when developing any new LC-MS method to analyze complex biological samples.
Minimization of 'dead volume' within the HPLC system is critical for optimum method performance. The dead volume is all of the volume in the system except for the column packing. The dead volume includes the volume contained in the injection system, tubing, frits, unions, other connections, and valves. Excess dead volume may

result in peak broadening and loss of resolution. Excess tubing, incorrect alignment of tubing with fittings, and increased number of connections and unions will increase dead volume. The length of tubing between the injector and the column is particularly critical and should be minimized as much as possible. Care should be taken when seating fittings and frits, because improper alignment can also cause mobile phase turbulence or mixing errors, resulting in retention time and peak area variation.

A mass spectrometer generates a voltage signal produced by ions striking the detector and depends on many different electronic settings within the instrument. Because the signal depends on different electronic settings, mass calibration and tuning are extremely important to ensuring optimal performance of the instrument, as analytical sensitivity can vary enormously based upon these parameters. An advantage of using SRM mode is that the mass spectrometer spends more time measuring the ions of interest than in full scan mode, enabling analysis with higher sensitivity. Even though operating in SRM mode will generally allow increased absolute signal for the analyte of interest compared to full scan mode, ion transmission through different parts of the mass spectrometer never reaches 100%. Therefore, fewer ions will pass through the second analyzer compared with the first. However, while obtaining the highest absolute signal for an analyte is desirable, it is not the end goal. A common method for measuring signal strength is to determine the S/N ratio of the analyte peak (see Figure 3).
Abbreviation: m/z, mass-to-charge ratio.
Figure 3. Contributions to the Signal Produced at the Detector of a Mass Spectrometer
In other words, the response of the detector is the signal (the counts at the top of the chromatographic peak [peak height] of the analyte of interest) and the baseline is the noise (the numerical counts value of the chromatographic baseline, not the zero baseline). When the signal is divided by the noise, the S/N ratio is obtained. Optimization of S/N ratio is significantly more important than optimizing the absolute signal intensity for the analyte(s) of interest.

Today, all LC-MS systems are managed by computers running software that allow for specialized data analysis. As part of this data analysis, the software employs algorithms that convert the detector output signal into meaningful qualitative or quantitative data, which is largely based on the number of data points collected across the chromatographic peaks and the correct integration of these peaks.
In order to define a chromatographic peak correctly, it is important to obtain enough data points across the peak. One hundred points across a peak fully defines the peak, but 20 data points are sufficient to adequately define a peak and also reduce the baseline noise. The minimum number, in order to prevent the lowering of peak heights and decreasing peak resolution if there are closely eluting peaks, is 10 data points. 23 This is particularly important when developing a multiplex assay with coeluting, or closely eluting, analytes. If the peaks are narrow, or there are many analytes (and IS) with the same retention time, then the scan speed and dwell times must be optimized to ensure that the minimum number of data points can be collected. The best practice recommendation is the collection of 15 to 20 data points across a chromatographic peak, with 10 points recognized as the absolute minimum necessary to define the chromatographic peak adequately for analyte quantitation.

chunks.text:
In LC-MS analysis, the number of data points collected across a peak is dependent upon the dwell time per ion transition (see Chapter 6.1). The dwell time is the amount of time spent by the mass spectrometer measuring a particular product ion and it is important to ensure that this is sufficient in order to collect enough data points across the peak. The intertransition delay time must also be taken into account. This is the time it takes for the mass spectrometer to clean the fragment ions out of the collision cell. In most mass spectrometers there is a default value that should not be changed by the user unless the user is trained to do this, but it is important that the user know this value. In the software for most mass spectrometers, it is up to the user to set the dwell time for each transition, and it is dependent upon the width of the chromatographic peak and the number of transitions that are being monitored. For scanning detectors (ie, for this particular type of detector), as the dwell time increases, the S/N ratio increases, thus improving sensitivity (see Figure 4). This does not apply to pulse counting detectors or SRM detection mode.
Abbreviations: m/z, mass-to-charge ratio; S/N, signal-to-noise.

As mentioned above, during method development, it is important to ensure that an adequate number of data points is collected across a chromatographic peak for a particular analyte, so a balance must be struck between the S/N ratio and the number of points as dwell time optimization is performed.
Once the data points across the peak are collected, it is necessary for the peak to be integrated. Integration determines the area, height, and retention time of the peak and thus enables subsequent data analysis, such as construction of standard curves and calculation of unknown concentrations of the analyte being measured. Additionally, no matter how capable the software, at this point, it does not match the skills of a chromatographer for accurate integration. Common integration errors can be seen in Figure 5.

The matrix components of a biological sample that are to be assayed by MS generally include salts, lipids, proteins, peptides, and organic small molecules. It is well known that any matrix component can interfere with or enhance the ionization of the analyte of interest in the mass spectrometric experiment. The most important matrix components that alter the ionization efficiency of the analyte of interest are salts and lipids, most specifically phospholipids. 57,58 While these molecules are present endogenously, it has recently been demonstrated that exogenous compounds can also be responsible. These include polymers from the plastic collection tubes, anticoagulants, and the gels used in plasma/serum separator tubes. 38 Most of the interfering matrix components can be removed during sample preparation and chromatographic separation.
The matrix can also include substances that will interfere with sample preparation. For example, analyte bound to high-affinity binding sites may be incompletely extracted, the pH or ionic strength of the sample may affect the partitioning of analyte during extraction, and the extraction efficiency of lipophilic compounds can be greatly affected by triglyceride concentrations. As a result, recovery experiments should be included soon after a successful LC-MS program has been identified.
Recommendations regarding evaluation of matrix effects are discussed in Chapter 6.7.2.

Product ion cross-talk in an LC-MS system may occur when two precursor ions (eg, A and B) give rise to product ions having the same m/z , regardless of whether A and B themselves have the same m/z . Product ion cross-talk is only of real concern when compounds enter the mass spectrometer at the same time (eg, chromatographic coelution or flow injection analysis as commonly performed in newborn screening laboratories). This is distinct from the interference of isobaric molecules that have identical product ions, which require chromatographic resolution for reliable quantitation. Product ion cross-talk occurs when the collision cell of the mass spectrometer is not completely emptied of product ions from compound A before it is subsequently filled with product ions from compound B. This interference results in the delivery of product ions from compound A to the detector and signal in the chromatographic trace for compound B, regardless of whether compound B is actually present in the sample (see Figure 6).
The phenomenon most commonly occurs when SRM dwell times and/or interchannel delay times are extremely short, (eg, < 1 millisecond). Manufacturers of mass spectrometers have implemented strategies to eliminate or minimize product ion cross-talk, even at very low SRM dwell times (< 5 milliseconds) without a concomitant drop
in signal intensity. These strategies include linear acceleration with axial ion ejection, traveling wave devices, pulsing of the RF-confinement field, and radial ion ejection. Even with these strategies in place, it is appropriate to evaluate for product ion cross-talk.

chunks.text: An easy method to monitor for product ion cross-talk involves the use of a 'dummy' SRM transition that shares a product ion with the analyte of interest (see Figure 6). If signal appears in the dummy transition at the same chromatographic retention time as the analyte of interest, then product ion cross-talk may be a problem. Increasing the interchannel delay time will eliminate cross-talk because the collision cell is given additional time to clear ions from the analyte of interest. Unrecognized interference from product ion cross-talk may be further minimized by monitoring multiple product ions for each precursor ion because the analyte of interest will produce product ions in the same ratio at different concentrations, and product ion cross-talk alters the ratio of product ions as the concentration of analyte is varied (see Chapters 4.3.1, 7.4, and 9.2.5, as well as CLSI document C50 1 ).

Accurate quantitation of analyte relies on high-quality standard materials. IS used to control for sample-tosample variability of ionization efficiency and calibration materials are either synthesized de novo or purified from natural sources. In both cases, compounds related to the primary substance of interest can be copurified. Ionpairing agents and other molecules can also be copurified because they are used to enhance compound stability or solubility. While impurities present in IS may not complicate analysis when there is no interference with the transitions being monitored, the gravimetric quantitation of standard material is compromised. Stable isotopelabeled analogs that are used as IS often include a small, often undetectable, proportion of partially labeled or unlabeled molecules. These impurities can also interfere with quantitation of the unlabeled analyte of interest. As a result, proper characterization of standard materials includes HPLC with photometric and mass spectrometric detection. Reports of these analyses are often available from the manufacturer (see CLSI document C50 1 ).

In order to assess the concentration of analyte in test samples, calibration of the analytical process is required through generation of a relationship between a known amount of analyte (concentration) and the analyte response function (peak area, peak height, or ratios of analyte to IS areas/heights). Calibration of quantitative MS assays is not to be confused with mass calibration of the spectrometer. The material from which calibration reagents are made should be of the highest available purity and have a COA describing the material's purity and methodologies used to assess such purity. 59 Certified reference standards are the preferred material. If certified reference standards are unavailable, then available calibration materials should be verified against proficiency testing (PT) samples and alternative methodologies when possible (see CLSI document EP32 60 ).
The process of calibration may be performed in two modes. The most common form of assay calibration for LC-MS assays involves isotope dilution, whereby calibrators of known concentration (and purity) are prepared, spanning the range of measurement. A structurally similar analog or stable (nonradioactive) isotopically labeled version of the test analyte is added at a single concentration (to all calibrators, samples, and QC materials) and a ratio of analyte peak area to the analog/isotopically labeled form (IS) is generated across the concentration range of measurement. The calibration response function is created as the response ratio of analyte peak area to IS peak (y-axis) vs the known concentration added (x-axis) to generate the calibration equation (y = bX + a for linear calibration plots). Test samples/QC peak area response ratio values are then back-calculated against the calibration equation to determine the amount of analyte present. The method should be rigorously evaluated such that the response ratios allow for normalization of analytical recovery across the milieu of possible biases that occur during sample extraction, chromatographic separation, ionization, and subsequent detection. It is important to consider incubation time after the IS is added, particularly when there is a significant amount of protein binding for the analyte of interest. If over-recovery occurs during method development, this may be due to insufficient time allocated for incubation of the IS with the test specimen.

chunks.text:
Alternatively, a stable isotope-labeled IS may be used as the reference response for the test analyte. 61 This mode of calibration does not require a calibration curve per se, but relies upon the addition of a known amount of IS and multiplying peak area ratio (analyte/IS) by an added concentration of IS to determine the original amount of test analyte. This protocol requires a greater degree of evaluation of the IS to ensure correct and complete labeling of molecules and assurance that, when using deuterated IS, hydrogen-deuterium exchange does not occur. In this instance, correlation of stable-labeled IS to equimolar-unlabeled analyte should be performed on a regular basis. It must be recognized that this approach to quantitation can significantly limit the linear range of the measurement system and is generally more affected by matrix effects than calibration using an external calibration curve with matrix-matched calibration materials.
Mass spectrometers are concentration-dependent instruments with limitations of linear range. Due to relative efficiencies in ionization (ie, source saturation) and detector restrictions (multiplier blinding), calibration models are generally determined using 'best fit' principles and have been historically limited to linear (preferred) or quadratic curves. Exponential curves, curves using power functions, or transformation of curves (logarithmic fitting), are generally not used for calibration in MS assays. Least squares regression analysis (1/x or 1/x ) is 2 historically used for LC-MS assays as a means of establishing best fit lines for calibration curves due to their homoscedastic (showing equal variance) nature. Weightings to standard curves (ie, 1/x, 1/x ) may be applied 2 when appropriate for the assay (when the data are heteroscedastic, ie, showing unequal variance). These principles will be described and explained in further detail below.

Calibration materials or calibrators, also known as analytical standards or calibration standards, are materials with known or assigned values, within a range of clinically relevant concentrations and characteristics (eg, specific clinically relevant form of an analyte) that are used to establish a numerical relationship between output or response of a measurement procedure with the response of a test specimen for a specific analyte. Calibrators may be purchased from a commercial source or may be prepared by the laboratory. Calibration materials should be evaluated for purity and the stability characteristics of the materials should be defined. Calibrator value assignments should be traceable to a reference measurement procedure, whenever possible. 59,62-64 A general procedure for establishing metrological traceability of calibrator value assignments can be found in CLSI document EP32 60  and ISO 17511. 5
Certified reference materials (CRMs) can be used to validate calibrator value assignments for commercial or in-house prepared calibrators. CRMs are available that contain 1) pure compound dissolved in solvent, or 2) pure compound dissolved into a biological matrix. The high degree of accuracy associated with CRM value assignments arises from the fact that the materials are value assigned using reference measurement procedures and are reported with a stated uncertainty.
CRMs that contain pure analyte in solvent may be used as spiking solutions to prepare matrix-appropriate calibrators. Preparation of calibrators by spiking pure compound into matrix-free solvent is not recommended unless the laboratory can demonstrate that the method does not suffer from matrix interference (see Chapter 6.5.1). Use of CRMs to prepare calibrators is preferred when possible because the resulting calibrator value assignments can be traced to a reference measurement procedure. However, this practice may not be practical due to the limited quantities of CRMs obtained during purchase.

Calibration materials should be evaluated for purity and the stability characteristics of the materials should be defined. Calibrator value assignments should be traceable to a reference measurement procedure, whenever possible. 59,62-64 A general procedure for establishing metrological traceability of calibrator value assignments can be found in CLSI document EP32 60  and ISO 17511. 5
Certified reference materials (CRMs) can be used to validate calibrator value assignments for commercial or in-house prepared calibrators. CRMs are available that contain 1) pure compound dissolved in solvent, or 2) pure compound dissolved into a biological matrix. The high degree of accuracy associated with CRM value assignments arises from the fact that the materials are value assigned using reference measurement procedures and are reported with a stated uncertainty.
CRMs that contain pure analyte in solvent may be used as spiking solutions to prepare matrix-appropriate calibrators. Preparation of calibrators by spiking pure compound into matrix-free solvent is not recommended unless the laboratory can demonstrate that the method does not suffer from matrix interference (see Chapter 6.5.1). Use of CRMs to prepare calibrators is preferred when possible because the resulting calibrator value assignments can be traced to a reference measurement procedure. However, this practice may not be practical due to the limited quantities of CRMs obtained during purchase.

Matrix-appropriate CRMs may be used for the purpose of assigning or validating calibrator values for in-house prepared or commercially purchased calibrators. For these purposes, the use of CRMs that are commutable with native patient samples is preferred. The commutability characteristics of CRMs may be found in published commutability studies. Preparation of calibrators by diluting matrix-appropriate CRMs into a different proxy matrix is not recommended unless the laboratory can demonstrate that the final preparation does not exhibit a matrix effect that differs from native matrix (see Chapter 6.5.1).
Whenever possible, the matrix used to prepare calibration materials should be identical to that of the matrix used for testing. For exogenous molecules, analyte-free biofluids are the acceptable calibrator matrix, preferably collected in the same manner as test specimen type (lithium heparin plasma, EDTA plasma, red top serum, etc.). For assays testing more than one matrix (ie, human plasma and human urine), demonstration of trueness of measurement in all applicable matrixes must be performed. In these instances, QC materials should represent the matrixes being tested in the assay; calibrators may be made in the matrix that posits the greatest medical risk or, in cases of equivalence, the matrix with the highest testing volume.
A 'proxy' matrix is often required for preparation of calibrators for endogenous analytes. These proxy matrixes are usually generated through removal of endogenous analyte by dialysis, stripping a native matrix with activated charcoal, or preparation of synthetic matrix materials. The goal of 'proxy' matrixes is the generation of calibration samples that: 1) are physiologically representative of the test matrix, thus minimizing matrix differences (matrix effects); and 2) have none or minimal concentration of analytes of interest and still retain as many physiological properties as possible. It is recommended that careful consideration of appropriate carrier materials (1% to 6% bovine serum albumin) or specific binding proteins be undertaken to ensure adsorptive losses and matrix effects are controlled (see CLSI document EP14 65 ). The design of a successful calibration scheme should take into consideration the basic measurement features of an assay, such as the LLMI and ULMI. It is not current best practice to determine limit of blank (LoB) and LoD for clinical verification of LC-MS assays in general, due to the low background noise inherent in LC-MS assays, and the variation in chromatographic peak shape through the repeated analysis of specimens. However, it should be noted, that where a clinical research assay is under development without a priori knowledge of the desired analytical measuring interval (AMI), LoB and LoD may be helpful as initial verification parameters before determining the desired LLMI and ULMI of the assay (see CLSI document EP17 68 ). The intent of this chapter is to define rigorously qualified limits of quantitation for the analytical measurement interval after the desired clinically relevant interval has been established.
The bounds of the measuring interval are defined by the LLMI and the ULMI. The LLMI is the lowest measurand concentration at which all defined performance characteristics of the measurement procedure are met. On the other end, the ULMI is the highest measurand concentration (without dilution) at which all defined performance characteristics of the measurement procedure are met. The methods used to derive and validate these limits are described elsewhere (see CLSI document EP17 68 ). The limits are germane to the calibration process because the calibration curves often include these limits in addition to a blank (standard containing matrix only) and a zero (matrix with IS) calibration standard. ULMI and LLMI must lie within the interval of linearity-the analytical range at which there is a defined relationship between the analyte concentration and the signal intensity. This is a distinction that is relevant to the clinical laboratory because the assay may achieve linearity at very high and low concentrations without having sufficient trueness and precision at the extremes. If this is the case, then the extremes of linearity are not commensurate with the rest of the clinical assay, so the clinical assay should operate within a narrower interval than the interval of linearity.

chunks.text: As mass spectrometric assays are typically calibrated using a linear fit, the recommendations for the number of calibration standards have been based on a linear fit. US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidelines state that a calibration should include a blank, a zero, and six to eight calibration standards 37 ; however, only nonzero standards are used to construct the calibration curve. 37 Practically, the number of calibration standards necessary to define the measurement range is a function of the breadth of the analytical curve and the defined medical decision points. Curves that represent ranges broader than three orders of magnitude (eg, 10 to 1000) or nonlinearity (quadratic) should incorporate additional standards to reproducibly describe the relationship between dose and response.

Mass spectrometric assays typically have a relatively broad quantitative range-approximately two to three orders of magnitude. This is because quantitation is based on ratios of ion intensities, and the precision of these ratios is highest when the ratios are around unity. For example, if the IS has a concentration of 1 ng/mL, then it is expected that the assay will behave best in the range of 0.1 to 10 ng/mL. If trueness is clinically necessary at values that differ by more than three orders of magnitude, then it may be necessary to have more than one analytical range for this analyte. This would involve a different concentration of IS and a different set of calibration standards to encompass the much higher or lower concentration range.
In practice, the calibration standards should be positioned at the LLMI and ULMI and at any medically relevant decision points within the analytical range. Additional calibration standards are placed over the calibration range; often stepping logarithmically from the maximum to minimum analytical concentrations, and this series of calibration standards may obviate the need for specifically designated clinical decision point calibration standards. The required points are necessary to ensure optimal calibration at concentrations that would lead to actionable values being reported.
The need for multiple analytical ranges and the number of clinical decision points is assay-dependent. Additionally, due to the variability in institutional clinical practices and patient characteristics, the analyte concentrations that trigger a clinical action also differ from one institution to another. Thus, it is important that the laboratory choose calibration standards at clinical decision points after consultation with the clinicians who will be using the results.

chunks.text: In current practice, laboratories generally perform calibration at the beginning of each batch of clinical samples. This differs from the practices of other analyzers in the clinical chemistry laboratory that may perform a full calibration biannually as required by regulatory guidance. 69 Some have demonstrated that the use of the response factor-the ratio of intensities from an equimolar mixture of IS and analyte-can obviate the need for full calibration with every batch of samples. 61 In the absence of good data demonstrating noninferiority of the new calibration scheme, the standard of practice is to calibrate with every batch of clinical samples. However, this should by no means be a requirement if a laboratory can demonstrate equivalent results with an alternative calibration frequency (see CLSI document EP15 70 ).

Best practice in the MS domain dictates processing at least six to eight nonzero calibrators each run, 37 and fitting to the calibration data a simple model which then serves as the basis for converting instrument response (eg, peak area) into a concentration estimate for each sample in that run. 37 It can also yield a valuable assessment of the estimate's imprecision or uncertainty, reflecting at least the repeatability sources of variation associated with the calibration data and curve-fitting process; this can be expressed as an SD (or standard error of the estimate [SEE]) or in the form of an interval estimate.
For a typical bioanalytical assay calibration, the simple model is a first- or second-degree polynomial; these correspond to a straight line (Y = bX + a) and parabola (Y = aX  + bX + c), respectively; and curve fitting is handled 2 by a weighted least squares algorithm built into the instrumentation's software. Therefore, the laboratory must choose from the available models and available weighting schemes. Both choices should be made in advance (not at run time), based on the assay's characteristic performance and the choice of calibrator concentrations. If the trajectory expected 'on average' for the calibrators in concentration-response coordinates is essentially straight, the first-degree polynomial is the appropriate model, whereas the second-degree polynomial model may be the best available expedient for coping with structural nonlinearity. (It may be questioned whether a parabola is the ideal shape to fit if curvature is expected only at high concentrations.)
Ordinary, unweighted least squares regression algorithms for fitting straight lines and parabolas assume something rarely true, namely, that the SDs of the calibrator responses are essentially constant across the measuring interval. This can be visualized as dispersion of roughly uniform thickness around the fitted curve when many replicates are processed for each calibrator. It is more common, especially for assays with a broad measuring interval, to encounter relatively narrow vertical scatter for the responses at low concentrations, and progressively wider scatter at higher concentrations.

This has consequences, sometimes for the accuracy of sample estimates, and always for the assessment of their uncertainty. In this situation, the highest calibrators have an unduly influential impact on the position and orientation of the fitted curve; hence, the responses observed for these calibrators, even when consistent with expectations for their imprecision, may sometimes lead to severely biased estimates, especially for lowconcentration samples. Moreover, the SEE (a statistic measuring the 'average' thickness of the vertical scatter around the fitted line) will always represent an underestimate for high concentrations and an overestimate for low concentrations; hence, the SEE-dependent assessment of a concentration estimate's imprecision or uncertainty may be badly distorted.
Weighting, in its various forms, is intended either to correct or to compensate for this nonconstancy of variance. The choice of calibrator concentrations itself can serve as a form of compensatory weighting, eg, adopting a more or less logarithmic distribution weights the curve towards the low end. Based on the choice of a weighting scheme-a very simple model of how response imprecision varies with response, or with concentrationweighted least squares regression analysis systematically reduces the influence of calibrators associated with inherently high response imprecision (SDs), by transforming the size of the vertical deviations of observed responses from fitted values in a concentration-dependent manner; it then determines the best-fitting curve as the one that minimizes the sum of the squared transformed deviations. MS software commonly includes two reasonable weighting options, sometimes labeled '1/x 2 ' and '1/x,' which assume that the change in response variability is roughly proportional to concentration or to its square root, respectively. These offer two different degrees (strengths) of compensation for nonconstant variance (heteroscedasticity). If the assay's 'variance function' has been characterized, 71 choose the weighting option that best mirrors it, and avoid overcompensation.

For any given assay, curve-generation approaches should be compared empirically in terms of their impact on the bias and imprecision of samples with known values; or, alternatively, in terms of their impact on total analytical error (the 'sum' of bias and imprecision), and in light of assay- and concentration-specific clinical requirements for imprecision and bias (or for total error). A definitive study would consist of many runs, performed over a time period sufficient to exercise all relevant sources of variation, with each run including a panel of samples with known values assayed as unknowns, independent of the curve-generation process. The samples-ideally patient samples, otherwise a subset of the assay's calibrators-should represent the concentrations or intervals of clinical interest. Simulated runs based on knowledge of the assay's response profile can serve as a valuable supplement to empirical studies of this kind. 72,73 The comparison entails applying two or more curve-generation approachesjoint selections for model, weighting function, calibrator concentrations (their number, placement and replication order), and so on-to the data generated in these runs, followed by calculating suitable concentration-based measures of bias and imprecision from results obtained for the panel members in each approach, optionally combining the bias and imprecision estimates into a measure of total error by some appropriate formula.
Examination of calibrator back-fit results (meaning concentration estimates for the calibrators derived from the curve they served to establish) and also certain byproducts of the regression analysis-notably the adjusted R-squared statistic -have sometimes been advocated as the basis for selecting an approach to curve generation. Even when compiled across multiple runs, discrepancies between assigned and back-fit values for calibrators serving in their native role-ie, as a basis for generating the calibration curve-will tend to underestimate both
the bias and imprecision induced for samples processed independently, as unknowns. Nevertheless, this does represent a good and efficient starting point for comparing curve-generation options.

These statistical analyses are better suited for monitoring the quality of run-specific curve fits, once experience with the chosen curve-generation approach has revealed the range of values expected for the statistic. 6.7 Preverification
Before a full verification of the method, it is desirable to include a preverification step as part of the method development process. In this step, some basic method performance parameters such as specificity and selectivity, impact of matrix effects, carryover, and repeatability precision are evaluated in order to determine whether or not the newly developed method is ready to move on to full verification. Preverification allows for a quick assessment of the assay performance before committing time, money, and other laboratory resources to a full method verification.

A specific measurement procedure is capable of differentiating or selecting the targeted analyte from its analogs, complex biological matrix, and interfering compounds. LC-MS assays are superior to HPLC analyses with alternative detection mechanisms and immunoassays with regard to selectivity or specificity due to the combination of LC separation and mass selection, particularly with SRM transition monitoring. However, interferences may still exist from endogenous and exogenous isobaric compounds. Furthermore, the LC-MS system itself including injector, line connection, tubing, column, ion source, or even the mass analyzer, can experience a build-up of interferents or target analyte that will introduce carryover or affect the assay specificity, and ultimately impact the trueness and precision of the assay. The sample extraction and derivatization procedure may also introduce contamination to the assay. The following aspects should be tested to demonstrate assay specificity and be monitored continuously throughout the verification period to show the ruggedness.
The first thing to confirm within the testing system (including sample processing and LC-MS) is that the method has low background noise allowable for the assay. Signal from a matrix-matched double blank sample (no analyte, no IS) reflects background in an LC-MS system. To avoid problems with assay sensitivity, background peaks should be absent or < 20% of the peak area for the analyte at the LLMI or ≤ 5% of the IS at the expected retention time. Quantitation of a double blank sample reflects the background in the whole testing system including sample processing. If analyzing an endogenous analyte and a stripped blank does not exist, a surrogate blank that is comparable to the sample matrix may be used instead.

chunks.text: As previously described, matrix effects may cause general assay or sample-specific effects such as reduced sensitivity or recovery due to ion suppression, or erroneous results due to the presence of interfering peaks. Therefore, the best practice for evaluation of matrix effects is a critical component of liquid chromatographytandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) method verification. It is recommended that matrix effects experiments should be conducted according to the hierarchical experimental design strategies described below. The percent matrix effect (%ME) can be converted into percent matrix bias by the following equation: Percent matrix bias = 100 - %ME. The percent matrix bias should be evaluated in the context of TEa. The percent CV (%CV) of the peak areas should also be evaluated to determine the magnitude for which the matrix contributes to assay imprecision. If the response imprecision is > 15.0%, further development is likely needed, as matrix effects are contributing significantly to assay imprecision.
Use of peak areas will describe the overall ion suppression or interference effect of matrix as compared to analyte in neat solvent. The laboratory should evaluate the extent of any observed ion suppression in the context of method sensitivity requirements.
To determine if the sample matrix affects the analyte response differently than the IS (ie, if the IS cannot correct for the matrix influence), the peak area ratios can be used in the above equations to calculate the normalized percent matrix bias. If the effect of the matrix is similar for the analyte and the IS, the normalized percent matrix bias will be significantly smaller than the %ME. In this case, matrix effects on method sensitivity need to be considered by the laboratory. However, if the normalized percent matrix bias exceeds preestablished acceptance criteria, nonspecificity due to matrix is probable. If method sensitivity or specificity do not meet preestablished acceptability criteria in the presence of matrix, then the sample preparation may need to be optimized such that matrix influences are reduced.
A limitation of the postextraction spike and recovery approach is that the interaction of the exogenously added analyte with extracted serum matrix components may differ from that of the endogenous analyte. In addition, the approach does not address matrix influences on extraction efficiency. Experimental design details for describing matrix influence on extraction efficiency can be found in CLSI document C50. 1

Matrix effects should be evaluated according to matrix admixing experiments described in CLSI document EP07. 75
In this experimental design strategy, different native matrix samples are mixed in several proportions. If significant sample-specific matrix effects are present, the observed results will not agree with the expected results. For example, the following samples are prepared:
100, %Matrix B = 0. 80, %Matrix B = 20. 50, %Matrix B = 50. 20, %Matrix B = 80. 0, %Matrix B = 100
At minimum, five native matrix admixing experiments should be performed. The effect of matrix may be evaluated by linear regression analysis performed by plotting the observed concentration on the y-axis and the expected concentration on the x-axis. In addition, bias vs the expected value (based on the proportion of each sample used in a mixture) can be calculated. More detail regarding minimum number of replicates and determination of acceptability criteria can be found in CLSI document EP07. 75
A limitation of this approach is that analyte concentration will likely change depending on the proportions used to prepare each mixture. Because bias and imprecision frequently change with concentration, quantitation of the specific contribution due to matrix effect may be difficult. In addition, this experimental design may not detect general ion suppression caused by the presence of matrix as compared to the absence of matrix. To evaluate general ion suppression, matrix-mixing experiments may be conducted whereby native matrix is mixed in proportion with a matrix-free material.

The matrix should be evaluated by performing a T-column infusion experiment.
In this experiment, analyte dissolved in solvent is directly infused into the mass spectrometer using a syringe pump. 78 Once a stable total ion count is achieved, an extracted matrix sample is injected concurrently by the HPLC system. If significant ion suppression due to matrix is present, an observable decrease in TIC of the direct infusion will be observed at the time point when the matrix components elute from the column. The signal obtained in the absence of a sample extract can be compared with the signal obtained when the extracted sample is injected for quantitation of the matrix effect for the transition being monitored.
This experiment is useful to identify the time points during chromatography when matrix components can suppress ionization. This information may be important because although matrix components might not normally interfere at the retention time of the analyte, matrix effects may cause problems if there is a shift in retention time into the affected chromatographic region, or if column resolution deteriorates. The limitations of the approach include technical difficulties with producing a similar quantity of infusion signal vs injection signal and difficulties with quantitation of the matrix effect (eg, measurement of peak height is required rather than peak area).
Methods to quantify the influence of ion suppression/enhancement are well described and include postcolumn T-infusion experiments and signal-recovery spiking experiments. Briefly, the T-infusion experiment involves the infusion of IS or analyte into the mass spectrometer along with the eluent from a chromatographic separation of a prepared sample. The recovered signal is then compared with that observed when performing HPLC separations

in a matrix-free blank. 79 For signal-recovery spiking experiments, IS or analyte is added into the sample after it has been prepared for the instrument and the signal recovered is compared with the signal observed from the analysis of a spiked, prepared matrix-free blank. 76

By definition, LC-MS comprises a continuous flow measurement system, as opposed to a random access analyzer, and as such is susceptible to correspondingly increased risk of sample carryover. While there is no generally accepted limit to the extent of carryover allowable in an analytical run, carryover should not significantly impact assay bias or precision. 37,80 The detector signal that is generated from the analysis of blank samples should be well below the LLMI, independent of the concentrations of analyte present in other samples in the same run. CLSI document EP10 81  provides a straightforward approach for preliminary evaluation of carryover that can be applied to LC-MS systems. Briefly, three concentrations of measurand spanning the AMI are analyzed in a specific sequence of 10 samples per run, one run per day, for five days. The results are assessed visually and statistically using multiple regression analysis (see CLSI document EP10 81 ).
Assessment of carryover using CLSI document EP10 81  is limited in two ways. First, it addresses carryover using only analyte concentrations within the measuring interval. In practice, samples with analyte concentrations exceeding this interval could significantly bias results in subsequent samples. Secondly, CLSI document EP10 81 does not assess the magnitude of carryover into blank samples. Most recent FDA guidance 37 indicates that one or more blank samples should be injected immediately after a high concentration sample in order to assess carryover. Testing an analyte concentration well above the measuring interval would be a more sensitive means of detecting carryover. In clinical or forensic toxicology settings, abnormally high concentrations of a toxin may be present in any particular sample within a run; therefore, preverification experiments should determine at what point carryover from such specimens may bias subsequent samples. In this approach, carryover can be determined by injecting extracted negative samples after samples with increasing concentrations of analyte. The best practice recommendation is that the carryover limit should be the highest concentration that does not carry over to the negative sample at or above 25% of the LLMI. If desired, the carryover limit can correspond with the ULMI. For samples above the ULMI, a blank injection is required immediately after that specimen to ensure that carryover will not affect subsequent specimens. Or, in the case of batch analyses, all samples analyzed after the potential carryover specimen must be analyzed after a blank specimen demonstrates no analytically significant carryover.

CLSI document NBS04 82  recommends alternating high concentration samples and blank samples at least five times, and that any peaks associated with the blank samples should be below the LoD. One recent publication 83 suggests injecting 10 replicates of a low-concentration sample, then alternately injecting 10 replicates each of high-concentration and low-concentration samples. In addition to visual inspection of the results, a  -test is then t used to compare the means of the two sets of low-concentration injections. This number of alternating replicates of high and low/blank samples may provide additional information about carryover in runs with large numbers of samples.
Carryover that is most likely to affect the method performance will be the result of analyte carried from the autosampler/injection mechanism, analytical column, or tubing and connections into subsequent samples. However, analyte contamination of any of the components of the MS detector itself may also be considered a form of carryover. This may occur when analyte is directly infused into the MS detector during tuning/ optimization (see CLSI document NBS04 82 ), hence the need to carefully validate and perform cleaning and maintenance of the MS detector, as well as autosampler and LC system. Both internal ion optics, as well as the ionization source, should be regularly maintained to avoid accumulation of analyte that may ultimately increase the noise level for specific transition(s) of interest in the measurement procedure.

Before evaluating the precision of an assay over multiple runs and days for a full verification, a simple repeatability (within-run) precision evaluation should be conducted at multiple points over the calibration range. If the assay does not demonstrate acceptable repeatability, then it is not likely to be acceptable over multiple runs and the analyst should return to the development steps and refine the method. Precision should be evaluated at the following three concentrations: 110% of the LLMI, 90% of the ULMI, and (LLMI + ULMI)/2. At each concentration, 20 replicates should be run and the following parameters calculated: SD ( σ ), %CV, and the percent recovery of the target value. If the %CV and percent recovery are determined to meet the fit-for-purpose criteria, then the assay is ready to move to the full verification process.

The performance requirements of an analytical method will be dictated by the intended use of the method. If multiple analytes will be measured at varying clinically relevant concentration ranges, then the analytical performance of each analyte must be evaluated to ensure that the method is sufficient for use in analysis of all analytes. It is best practice to perform preverification experiments as described in Chapter 6.7 before the start of a full verification of a method.
The robustness of the method should be considered during verification to assess the impact of small changes such as temperature or humidity fluctuation, preparation of calibrator materials by different operators, instrument cleanliness, and incubation times. 84 Significant observed performance changes may warrant method reoptimization and repeat of method verification studies.
It is best practice to complete a full verification of a method before use. However, if using an FDA-approved kit on an FDA-approved platform, then, at a minimum, a partial verification is needed. If an FDA-approved kit is being used on a non-FDA-approved platform, or matrix (specimen), a full verification is strongly encouraged.
Acceptance criteria must be established for each component of the assay verification before beginning the verification data collection. Acceptable criteria can be based on biological variation, clinical guidelines established by expert groups, and local or regional regulatory requirements. Any acceptance criteria or evaluation parameters specified in this guideline are recommendations for intralaboratory verification. Additional studies may be required for regulatory submission.

chunks.text: The LLMI is the lowest actual amount of an analyte that can be reliably detected and meets the laboratory's requirements for trueness and precision. At a minimum, it is recommend that the LLMI meet a stated acceptable precision (eg, CV < 20%) and trueness (eg, < 15% bias), under stated experimental conditions. 37 An approach to determine LLMI can be found in CLSI document EP17. 68 LLMI verification experiments require a minimum of 40 replicates from three to five different samples close to the predetermined LoD, over at least five runs. This approach ensures that for samples with a true value equal to the LLMI, there is an approximate 95% probability that the test result will be sufficiently accurate. These parameters are the recommended criteria for intralaboratory evaluation. Performance targets may be different for regulatory submission.

Allowable dilutions that yield true results within and outside the measuring interval require verification. Due to the critical influence of specimen matrix on LC-MS separation and ionization chemistry, chosen diluents should be matrix appropriate in all cases outlined below. Both the intended dilution buffer and the dilution procedure should be validated. Analyte-free native matrix is preferred for dilution when available.
Dilution verification should employ replicate analysis and recovery assessment, as described in CLSI document EP15, 70 and as suggested by the European Medicines Agency. 84  Analyte recovery analysis is central to determining the suitability of a diluent, and the degree of allowable dilution in a measurement procedure. At concentrations greater than three times the LLMI, recoveries of 100 ± 15% are acceptable. Recoveries exceeding this parameter suggest skew due to overdilution, inappropriate diluent matrix, and/or matrix effects (eg, adsorptive losses) introduced by the intended diluent 84 (see CLSI documents C50 1 and EP15 70 ).
The following three scenarios, which call for dilution of specimens for various reasons, may all be validated using an 'integrity of dilution' approach. For any integrity of dilution experiment, at least five separate replicates of each intended dilution are prepared and the measurement procedure performed on each replicate sample. Specific approaches are described in corresponding subchapters. In general, mean recovery/trueness ± 15% of the nominal analyte concentration is acceptable. Additionally, imprecision ≤ 15% is acceptable. However, it is important to note that the specific criteria for acceptable recovery and imprecision following dilution may vary depending on the clinical application. These parameters are the recommended criteria for intralaboratory evaluation. Performance targets may be different for regulatory submission.

For occasions when specimens that contain analyte concentrations greater than the ULMI are submitted, dilution of the submitted specimen to achieve analyte concentrations within the linear measuring interval may be necessary. Again, specimen extracts (rather than neat specimens) are usually diluted, then assayed. However, in this case, the diluent should contain the same concentration of IS as the extract sample before dilution.
Verification of foreseeable, clinically applicable dilutions for analyte concentrations outside the ULMI requires determination of out-of-range results by an alternate measurement procedure. One should note that such procedures may be difficult to identify or access-if they are available at all-and results may not correlate directly to the in-house procedure. Thus, recovery analysis of the diluted specimen results may prove challenging. When maximal allowable dilutions yield analyte concentrations that are still outside the measuring interval, the result should be reported as a 'greater-than' result, similar to the reporting of results below the LLMI. However,
for patient populations in which very high analyte concentrations require monitoring for therapeutic response (ie, tumor markers), such practice diminishes the clinical utility of the measurement procedure, and clear communication to care providers should accompany the report.

Low-volume specimens (eg, pediatric short-draws, which routinely yield only 25 to 50 µL of serum) may require dilution to achieve minimum analytical volume requirements and assure accurate and precise result reporting. Such specimens may result from populations with different physiology, or complicated disease states that present inherent matrix differences from the standard testing specimen mix. These specimens may require an altogether different diluent matrix.
In low-volume specimens, the dilution usually occurs before extraction in order to bring specimen volume up to that required for the assay. Such dilutions require careful documentation of specimen and diluent volume for correct extrapolation of analyte concentration. Care should be taken, in such instances, to achieve adequate and appropriate volume expansion without diluting analyte concentrations to < 3 · LLMI. If dilution in such cases yields analyte concentrations < 3 · LLMI, it is likely that the entire native specimen has been consumed, and no repeat analysis can be performed. Thus, in these instances, placement of similarly diluted, well-characterized calibrator and/or QC concentrations in the analytical run with concentrations between the LLMI and 3 · LLMI can provide some basis for determining result acceptability, as long as the matrix is comparable.

General guidance to estimate imprecision is available in CLSI document EP05. 74 Assay developers should refer to the considerations for manufacturers in CLSI document EP05, 74 as the requirements for verification are not sufficient for assay validation by manufacturers. Precision studies should be conducted to evaluate repeatability (within run) and reproducibility imprecision for laboratory-developed tests. It is important to note that the evaluation of imprecision should include the entire testing process, including sample collection and storage, pretreatment, extraction, and analysis. Information regarding the magnitude of each component not only provides important insight for effective management of the assay, but also helps identify the sources of variation for troubleshooting purposes.
The test materials should represent the characteristics of the appropriate clinical specimen (eg, serum); stable patient sample pools are preferred. When necessary, such testing materials may also be purchased through a commercial source (eg, control materials). Additional matrix information of those control materials is also helpful to understand the matrix discrepancy between the clinical specimen and control materials (see CLSI document EP14 65 ). Knowledge of the stability over the course of the experiment is essential.
The concentration of the testing materials should be chosen carefully to span the AMI and also include samples at and within ± 25% of the medical decision point. If the high concentration pool and low concentration pool do not span the required interval, spiking of the pure standard may be appropriate. Likewise, the low-concentration pool may be diluted. In both cases, potential matrix effect needs to be taken into consideration.
At a minimum, the imprecision of each concentration should not exceed 15% CV except for the LLMI, where ≤ 20% CV is acceptable. 37 However, the imprecision measure should also consider the TEa of each analyte at the medical decision level as specified by regulatory guidance, 69 and an appropriate precision goal (ie, TEa/3) should be set accordingly. Additionally, acceptable criteria based on biological variation, clinical guidelines established by expert groups, and local or regional regulatory requirements should be considered. These parameters are the recommended criteria for intralaboratory evaluation. Performance targets may be different for regulatory submission.

chunks.text: Although LC-MS/MS methods using SRM tend to be more selective than other techniques such as immunoassays, interferences during mass spectrometric detection may still occur. CLSI document EP07 75 provides detailed information on interference testing procedures, as well as recommendations for the analysis and interpretation of interference testing results. It should be noted that the list of potential interferences in this document is extensive and interference testing should be relevant to the patient population that will be tested with a given assay. In addition, disease- or patient population-specific medications or interferents not included in CLSI document EP07 75  should be considered for testing. Additionally, any observed bias should be interpreted, along with how clinically relevant the bias would be on the concentration of the analyte. In LC-MS assays, interference testing is usually accomplished by adding a known, high concentration of the potential interfering substance to be tested into the matrix that the analyte will normally be measured in (eg, serum, urine, saliva), both with and without the analyte, and running this sample on the assay. For endogenous substances, the highest reported clinically relevant concentration should be tested. For drugs or other exogenous substances, concentrations 10fold higher than the highest concentration encountered after a therapeutic dose or patient exposure should be tested. For additives in patient specimen collection tubes, concentrations five-fold higher than the recommended concentration should be tested (see CLSI document EP07 75 ) in order to determine if these compounds may have a positive or negative impact on measuring the true analyte concentration.

chunks.text:
Potential interferences include over-the-counter medications, commonly administered or prescribed drugs and their metabolites, nutritional supplements, endogenous compounds, the sample matrix, high concentrations of hemoglobin, bilirubin or lipids, anticoagulants, clot activators, preservatives as well as the gel materials found in serum, or plasma separators in blood collection tubes (see Chapter 5.1.4). 47,85,86 Best practice is to use patient samples with high concentrations of these potential interferences and not to artificially add these into the correct matrix. Additionally, it is not necessary to continue to test increasing concentrations of interferences until obtaining an effect, such as a biased result, from a given interference. It is only necessary to try high values that are seen in the laboratory. At a minimum, a laboratory should test the commonly used tube types at the institution, triglycerides, hemolysis, and bilirubin. However, the laboratory should also be mindful that interference testing should always be relevant to the patient population to be tested with the assay. It is important to note that not all potential interfering substances may be available for spiking studies, so an evaluation of trueness using patient samples (see Chapter 7.5.1) from the patient population to be tested is recommended, even if the analyte must be spiked.
If the molecular weight of a potential interference is close to that of the analyte of interest, it is important to check for potential adduct formation (eg, sodium, ammonium, potassium) 87,88 or potential losses (eg, hydrogen chloride, water). Additionally, isomeric or isobaric compounds should also be evaluated for their potential to cause interference and should be chromatographically separated from the analyte of interest if they do cause interference 89 (see Chapter 6.4.2, as well as CLSI document C50 ). One example of this features the isomeric 1 branch amino acids: leucine, isoleucine, and alloisoleucine. In a flow injection newborn screening method, these amino acids are detected together along with 4-hydroxyproline. For diagnosis of and monitoring of maple syrup urine disease, complete separations of leucine, isoleucine, and alloisoleucine are necessary; otherwise, the patient's dietary treatment cannot be properly guided.

chunks.text: The trueness of a measurement procedure is defined as the closeness of agreement between a test result or measurement result and the true value. A central component of a test method relies on accurate establishment of its calibrator concentration, its traceability, and its degree of measurement uncertainty.  Once an MS method 6 is established, its trueness can be accessed through conduction of recovery, method comparison analyses, and/or analysis of the materials with assigned values. Assessment of trueness using more than one approach is recommended, to ensure that any 'hidden' sources of error are uncovered. Patient specimens should be used when available or following the hierarchy of: authentic patient specimens > pool of patient specimens > serumbased QC > aqueous nonbiological solutions. Acceptable criteria should be defined, based on biological variation, clinical guidelines established by expert groups, and local or regional regulatory requirements. When comparisons do not meet these criteria, assessment of calibrators, as well as selectivity of the method, should be evaluated as potential sources of bias.

chunks.text:
When available, a comparison to a higher order reference method (see CLSI document EP32 60 ) using a minimum of 40 samples, preferably patient samples (see CLSI document EP09 90 ) is recommended to assess the trueness of a method. Samples should cover the entire AMI and be obtained from the 'intent to test' population. Forty is the minimum number of samples for intralaboratory evaluation. Other numbers may be required for regulatory submission.
In situations in which only routine methods are available, rather than a standard reference method, difference in results of method comparison is simply a level of difference, not bias (see CLSI document EP09 90 ). Results of this type of method comparison cannot be used for trueness assessment; rather, they provide useful information for transferring reference intervals from one measurement procedure to the newly developed MS procedure. In addition, correlation analyses between MS and immunoassays may not be suitable for assessing trueness of newly developed MS procedures as many immunoassays have shown lack of specificity, and, in turn, trueness, for many analytes.

chunks.text:
When reference materials and/or methods are not available to assess the trueness of a measurement procedure, a spike and recovery analysis can be made. This approach can be used before the purchase of expensive reference materials and/or collaboration with a higher order reference laboratory to determine performance of a method with regards to trueness. It is recommended, at a minimum, to complete this analysis by spiking known standards into QC or patient samples at three clinically relevant concentrations over the concentration range of the method and determine the concentration with at least five replicates. 76 The deviation of the determined concentration from the expected concentration (endogenous concentration of analyte in the sample, plus the known concentration of the spike) can be used to determine trueness. In order to assess the recovery of an analyte in an assay, the ratio of the result obtained in an analysis of the material (which has been extracted from a biological matrix), to the actual quantity of the analyte present in, or added to, the matrix is calculated and expressed as a percentage (see CLSI document C50 1 ). In quantitative analyses of drugs, proteins, peptides, etc. in biological matrixes such as blood, serum, or urine using LC-MS methods, recovery is usually not 100%; therefore, new methods should be validated for consistency and reproducibility of recovery. Decreases in recovery may result from losses during sample preparation processes such as dilution, extraction, and filtration. Endogenous substances in the sample matrix can compete with analyte for binding sites in SPE resulting in incomplete removal of the analyte from the matrix. These substances can also coelute with analyte in LC and contaminate the ionization chamber of the mass spectrometer resulting in ion suppression or ion enhancement.
For verification of a bioanalytical method, recovery experiments should be performed at three concentrations (low, medium, and high) to verify that results obtained on extracted samples correspond with responses on directly injected samples that represent 100% recoveries. 37 Alternatively, when a QC sample is prepared by adding a calculated quantity of the analyte of interest to a biological matrix that already contains an endogenous amount of the analyte, the technique of standard additions should be used to determine the recovery efficiency. PT samples, QC samples, and external reference samples should be included in the recovery study.

The QMS is comprised of the policies and procedures that enable a laboratory to meet its stated quality goals. Two critical components of a laboratory's QMS include QA and QC. QA procedures for LC-MS assays must monitor the entire testing process from the preexamination phase through reporting and interpretation of results. QC plans must provide ongoing LC-MS method performance evaluation to ensure proper calibration and that measurement uncertainty remains appropriate for the intended medical use. Quantitative LC-MS methods may employ specimen preparation or pretreatment steps such as dilution, derivatization, hydrolysis, extraction, addition of IS, and concentration procedures. In order for QC processes to adequately monitor the entire analytical measurement phase, QC materials must be tested using the same procedures as patient samples. Furthermore, QC materials must be subjected to all pretreatment procedures.
Minimum quality requirements must be defined for each LC-MS method. QC requirements should be developed with consideration of the intended use of the method and may be based on TEa limits, expected biological variation, or risk associated with medical use of results (see CLSI documents C24 92 and EP23™ 93 ). General QA and QC guidelines have been published 94  (see CLSI documents EP23, 93 QMS01, 95 QMS06, 96 and QMS12 97 ) and are beyond the scope of this document. The following chapter is limited to aspects of QA and QC that may be considered unique to LC-MS testing.

8.1 Selection of Quality Control Materials
Two primary considerations when selecting QC materials for LC-MS assays are:
· The composition of the QC material matrix
· The stability of the QC material

chunks.text:
QC processes for LC-MS assays must monitor key method performance characteristics such as calibration validity, extraction efficiency, column performance, and magnitude of ion suppression. These performance parameters commonly depend on the composition of the sample matrix 98  (see CLSI document C50 1 ). QC materials with matrixes that differ substantially from that of patient samples may be ineffective for identification of LC-MS performance parameters that are unacceptable for test samples that consist of patient matrix. Therefore, the composition of the QC material matrix should resemble the patient sample matrix as closely as possible.
Commercially available QC materials may be used if they are matrix appropriate. However, commercial materials for analytes of interest for some LC-MS assays may not be available. For those that are available, the materials are usually designed for use with immunoassay methods. Because immunoassay methods often do not exhibit the large analytical measurement ranges achievable for LC-MS methods, optimal QC concentration ranges may not be represented in the commercial materials.
Use of pooled patient samples that contain endogenous analyte, or pooled samples spiked with exogenous analyte, may be used as QC material. Basic assessment of QC material stability characteristics is critical for using QC values for the purpose of monitoring method performance. Improperly stored or degraded QC materials are unacceptable for this intended use. If the laboratory prepares its own QC materials, the laboratory must perform a study to determine the appropriate storage conditions and stability requirements of the material.
If QC material stability requirements are determined by the laboratory, the following information should be documented: storage condition(s), concentrations tested, magnitude of changes observed over different time intervals, and the criteria used to determine if stability is acceptable. If QC materials will be subjected to freezethaw cycles, then the magnitude of the effect for the maximum number of freeze/thaw cycles should be determined. In addition, short-term stability of the QC material at ambient temperature should be evaluated for the time interval required for sample preparation and analysis. Experimental design details for evaluation of QC material freeze-thaw stability as well as short-term and long-term temperature stability, are available. 37 Protocols for handling of QC materials (eg, thawing procedures) should be included in the laboratory's procedure.
Stability and storage information provided by the manufacturer of commercial QC materials may be used if the manufacturer provides sufficient data regarding verification of the stability requirements. In this case, manufacturer-provided storage instructions must be strictly followed. If the laboratory modifies a commercial QC product (eg, a dilution is made to prepare a lower concentration material) or stores the material differently than the manufacturer recommends, the laboratory must validate the storage requirements and stability characteristics.
