According to regulatory guidance, 69 for quantitative tests, a minimum of two concentrations of QC must be measured at least every 24 hours during patient testing. However, more than two concentrations of QC may be required for LC-MS/MS assays. A unique consideration for LC-MS assays is the capability of the AMI to span many orders of magnitude. If the method AMI is large, an increased number of QC concentrations may be needed to reliably assess method performance over the interval. For example, the measurement of testosterone requires the inclusion of multiple decision thresholds (for both males and females) and, therefore, would require additional concentrations of QC materials.
The recommended practice is to place QC concentrations at or near significant medical decision points to aid in the detection of clinically significant errors. Ideally, QC concentrations should cover the entire analytical measurement interval, including coverage near the assay ULMI and LLMI. The concentrations should be evenly spaced across the AMI to ensure adequate method performance for all measured values, and to establish that assay linearity has not changed. 37 A minimum of three QC concentrations are recommended: one at

approximately three times the LLMI, one near the middle of the measuring interval, and one near the ULMI. chunks.text: An increased number of QC measurements (greater than two concentrations analyzed per 24 hours) may be required if the dynamic range of the assay is large, or if a relatively large number of samples are analyzed during a single run. For best practice, the number of QC samples analyzed during a batch should represent at least 5% of the total number of patient samples or, at a minimum, six QC samples total (eg, three concentrations of materials analyzed in duplicate during the run). However, the frequency of QC analysis required for the method should ultimately reflect method performance established during method verification, the number of samples analyzed over a specified time period, and the clinical impact of an erroneous result. QC frequency should be continuously reassessed during routine clinical production. Less frequent analysis of QC may be indicated if the method is found to be stable. Alternatively, increased analysis of QC is indicated if the method is found to exhibit issues with degradation of performance. Placement of QC samples should optimize detection of analytical shifts, drifts, or errors during any part of an analytical run. A common practice is to place QC samples at the beginning, middle, and end of an analytical run for analyses with large samples batches, eg, > 50 specimens. For methods that are analyzed in continuous access mode, QC should be analyzed at a frequency sufficient to method shifts or drifts such that the potential release of erroneous results is unlikely. Use of QC trend rules and multirules may improve timely detection of method performance degradation (see CLSI documents C24 92  and QMS01 95 ).

chunks.text: The purpose of the system suitability test is to evaluate the performance of the LC-MS system before the analytical run (see Chapter 9.2.1). A nonextracted sample (eg, analyte or internal standard in pure solvent) is used to confirm that basic instrument performance parameters are within expectations. This sample provides system performance information that is independent of extraction. The SSS should be analyzed after the instrument has equilibrated and several priming injections have been performed. The SSS should be analyzed at least three times and the first injection result should be discarded. The acceptability criteria should include basic chromatography parameters established during method verification, such as the presence of correct peaks, intensity of background and analyte signal, peak resolution, retention time, and peak symmetry. Failure of the system suitability test may indicate a problem with system performance and should be investigated. Analysis of the SSS is recommended at minimum before each analytical run and following preventive maintenance, loss of vacuum, or when system equilibration has been compromised.

A double blank sample refers to an extracted sample that does not contain analyte or IS. The purpose of double blank sample is to monitor the background signal in the LC system and mass spectrometer, as well as to assess carryover from the preceding analysis, or after a high concentration sample. Injection of double blank samples at the beginning and end of an analytical batch, as well as after a high calibrator or QC samples, is recommended. The absence of a peak at the analyte-specific transitions, or a peak area < 20% of the LLMI, is recommended to confirm that the system is free of background noise or carryover. The peak area for the IS transition should be ≤ 5% of the peak area for a sample containing IS.
The blank sample refers to an extracted sample that contains IS but no analyte. The purpose of the blank sample is to determine the contribution of degraded IS to the analyte peak area (eg, due to hydrolysis of IS deuterium moieties). The analyte transition peak area of the blank sample should be < 20% of the LLMI for the analyte. A blank sample should be analyzed, at minimum, during the beginning and end of each batch.

chunks.text:
One advantage of LC-MS methods is the ability to measure multiple analytes (eg, hormone or drug panels) using a single injection of sample. QC materials for such multicomponent methods should include appropriate concentrations for each analyte, as discussed in Chapter 8.2.1. QC acceptability criteria should be established for each analyte included in the assay. If the analytes are not directly related, QC failure for one analyte does not typically require rejection of the other analytes measured in the assay. However, if the assay includes a parent drug in addition to its metabolites, all results should be rejected if QC fails for either the drug or any of its metabolites.
Multiplexing systems have become available in which two or more LC columns are used within an analytical run to increase LC-MS sample throughput. If the system contains two separate sample delivery modules (eg, two injectors, two separate HPLC systems), each delivery module should be considered a separate system and should be subject to control. Therefore, each delivery system and column should include calibrators and QC. Some systems are configured such that the samples share a common injection and delivery system, but the sample delivery streams are switched between columns immediately before the column. Common practice is that a portion of the calibrators are analyzed on each column, with the complete calibration curve determined from combining results from both columns. In this case, the run order should be scheduled such that every concentration of QC is analyzed on each column.
To detect a problem with an individual column, it is preferable that aliquots of the same extraction or final sample preparation of QC materials are used to evaluate column agreement. Comparison of Levey-Jennings charts or other means of QC shift or drift detection mechanisms should be used to assess column comparability over time. Reagent lot change validations for calibrators, QC, and reagents should include each column.

chunks.text: Mass calibration and tuning of the mass spectrometer are typically performed at the same time. Mass calibration refers to the process of assigning accurate mass values to specific ion peaks and is accomplished through injection of a solution of mass calibration standards. Tuning refers to the process of adjusting instrument parameters such as voltages and gas flow to optimize peak intensity. If the mass spectrometer is not properly calibrated or tuned, significant loss of analytical sensitivity and/or specificity may occur. Mass calibration and tuning, or validation of calibration/tuning, should be performed every six months or according to the manufacturer's recommendations. Mass calibration and tuning should be performed more frequently if the mass calibration is not stable. Each laboratory must establish the minimum frequency for mass calibration/tuning and acceptability criteria for allowable total ion count, ion intensity, peak resolution, and mass shift. Mass calibration and tuning should be performed or verified after major maintenance, environmental change, instrument failure, or when instrument vacuum is compromised.

Often the same assay is performed on multiple LC-MS systems. Each LC-MS system should be considered unique, even if the additional instruments are from the same manufacturer and are the same model. The best practice for implementation of an established and verified assay on another LC-MS system would include all method verification procedures described in Chapter 7. However, according to regulatory guidance, 69 a more limited verification of the assay may be acceptable. Limited or 'partial' verifications must be 'fit for purpose' and are justified only if the likelihood of substantial differences in the method performance is low. The limited verification may range from evaluation of LLMI, trueness, precision, and analytical measurement interval to a full verification as described in Chapter 7, and implementation is at the discretion of the laboratory director.
Instrument-to-instrument correlations should be performed at least every six months. Acceptability criteria should be based on method performance criteria and clinical use of the results.

NOTE: This chapter refers to a new column purchased from the same manufacturer and of the same stationary phase type as the column used during initial method verification. The column may or may not have a new lot number. Use of a different stationary phase, or a column from a different manufacturer, would require a new method verification.
Installation of a new chromatography column, whether from the same or different manufacturer's lot, should be considered a reagent lot change. Procedures to verify the performance of a new column must demonstrate whether the new column can produce results similar (within allowable variation) to those obtained with the previous column. The validation can be conducted by analyzing a minimum of five previously analyzed matrixappropriate patient samples without changing any HPLC or MS conditions, except for replacement of the old column with a new one. The concentrations of the patient samples used to verify a new column should span the analytical measurement interval. If patient samples cannot be obtained, an independent linearity assessment should be performed (see CLSI document EP06 66 ). Guidelines for validation of new reagent lots are available. 99 The results from the new column should be compared with those from the old column and acceptability criteria should be based on preestablished chromatographic acceptability criteria (eg, retention time, background signal, peak area/height, resolution and absence of incorrect peaks) and method performance requirements.

New lots of QC materials, calibrator, and reagents must be verified for clinical use (see CLSI document C24 92 ).
New lots of commercial calibrators or new preparations of in-house calibrators must be validated to ensure that patient sample results will not change by a clinically significant amount due to use of the new calibrator preparation. New calibrator lots may be validated by analyzing a group of patient samples at a time when the method was calibrated using the old lot of calibrators. The same patient samples are then reanalyzed when the method is calibrated using the new lot. The difference in patient results for the old vs new lot can then be compared to predetermined acceptability criteria based on method performance expectations established during method verification. Alternatively, the new lot of calibrators may be analyzed as unknown samples when the method is calibrated using the old lot. The magnitude of difference between the observed results vs expected values for the new lot may then be compared against acceptability criteria. Validation of the traceability of a new lot of calibrators is recommended (see Chapter 8.7.5).
New lots of reagents must be validated for clinical use. It is often difficult to determine what constitutes a 'new lot of reagents' for LC-MS assays. For example:
· Should a new lot of formic acid or ammonium formate for preparation of mobile phase constitute a 'new reagent lot' if all other components of the mobile phase remain the same?
· Should every new preparation of mobile phase be considered a new lot if the preparation is made strictly according to procedure and lot numbers of components do not change?

Best practice is for each laboratory to define a 'new lot of reagent' based on the expected consequences of changing a reagent component on method performance. For example, a new lot of base powder used to prepare an extraction reagent may have the potential to significantly affect method performance. Therefore, the laboratory may wish to define this as a reagent lot change. 64 The COA for all lots of reagent components and columns used for a method should be maintained by the laboratory. In addition, the initial dates of use for all new lots of reagent components should be documented.

LC-MS methods commonly require multiple steps that require transfer of samples before analysis such as derivatization, extraction, centrifugation, and addition of sample to an autosampler vial. Sample identification integrity must be maintained throughout the process to ensure the result is applied to the correct patient's medical record. Some laboratories have implemented automated sample preparation with specimen identification and tracking capability. However, the process remains largely manual for many laboratories. The laboratory must develop and document a system to label or reliably track the identification of all aliquots and autosampler vials. In addition, sample identification must be linked with run order and be maintained such that the laboratory can access the raw data for a specific patient sample, calibrator, or QC material.

Monitoring of LC-MS/MS systems and associated methods, once put into clinical use, is important for both regulatory compliance and minimization, identification, and correction of analytical errors. Scheduling of routine and comprehensive monitoring ensures optimum LC-MS system and method performance.
For LC-MS systems, manufacturer recommendations for maintenance should be followed and incorporated into SOPs. Importantly, maintenance schedules and frequencies may not only need to occur more often than manufacturer's recommendations, but may also vary between laboratories. These frequencies depend on various testing aspects that include, but are not limited to:
· Sample type (eg, whole blood, serum, plasma, and urine)
· Sample pretreatment protocols
· Testing volumes
· Ionization sources used
Users of LC-MS systems should not rely solely on the manufacturer for guidance/direction regarding maintenance. Routine preventive maintenance can and should be performed by laboratory personnel trained in the use of LC-MS systems, following recommendations from the manufacturer and laboratory director (see CLSI document C50 1 ).
Postimplementation monitoring of LC-MS/MS-associated methods, such as PT and system performance monitoring, is important for ensuring method robustness and result quality. The following chapter describes the various components of both LC-MS/MS system and method monitoring postimplementation.

One of the most preferred methods for assessing assay quality is through the use of an external quality assessment (EQA) program. Participation in an EQA program enables a laboratory to compare its performance against other laboratories using similar methods, reagents, and instruments.
Users should refer to CLSI document QMS24 101  for detailed instructions on how to use PT to improve clinical laboratories. Laboratories participating in EQA should be aware of any methodological differences in their assay compared with other participating laboratories. Specifically, with respect to MS-based assays, differences in assay calibration material, SRM transitions, ionization conditions, mobile phases, sample pretreatment protocols, and chromatographic conditions may cause systematic or random differences between results. In general, EQA programs use an acceptability criterion of ± 3 SDs of the all-method mean and/or peer group mean. Besides passing the EQA challenges, laboratories should closely monitor their performance in these programs to look for trends or shifts in their assay (eg, note whether results are always on one side of the mean). The use of CRMs or NIST standards (where available) may aid in the laboratory's investigation of discordant results.

For many low-volume or esoteric analytes, there are no available EQA schemes in which to participate. In addition, even if several different laboratories perform testing on the same analyte, they may not make up a statistically significant peer group for statistical analysis. In these situations, a laboratory should design and implement an alternative assessment procedure (AAP). Each laboratory should define the frequency of performance and procedures for evaluation of results. Consideration should be given to (but not limited to) the specimen source, the limits of acceptability, and the range of concentrations tested before performing the procedure. An external laboratory may be used as part of an AAP, provided it can measure the correct analyte in the appropriate matrix.
If an external laboratory is used, it is preferable that the same or very similar methodology be employed for proper comparison. Although it is not mandatory that the other laboratory perform the same methodology, if the methods are not based on the same methodology, the correlation between the two should be documented. Refer to CLSI document QMS24 101  for detailed instructions on how to perform assessments of laboratory tests when EQA is not available. 102

Before beginning each run, throughout the analysis of samples, and at the end of batch analysis, SSS should be injected to ensure that the chromatographic system(s) and mass spectrometer are functioning together as expected. It is important that SSS materials are evaluated for stability and optimal storage conditions to ensure the quality of that material over time. Documented results should meet established acceptance criteria before patient samples are tested and/or resulted. Laboratories should consider setting acceptance criteria for variables such as retention time, peak height and width, ion ratios, and S/N ratio. It has been recommended that seven system suitability injections be used in the beginning of each run. 103 However, a minimum of 3 samples should be run (Chapter 8.3.1), with the first injection discarded. If seven are used, five of the seven SSS should be samples with concentrations at the upper end of the analytical measurement interval of the assay or at high QC concentrations. The analyte/IS peak area ratios that are obtained for the SSS analyzed in replicates must have a CV < 6%. The five high concentration samples are followed by a blank sample extract or mobile phase solution. This can be used to evaluate system carryover. The permissible concentration of carryover is defined by using an FDA recommendation that requires the signal in blanks to be < 0.2 of the LLMI for the analyte. 37 A low concentration sample with concentrations at the lower end of the analytical measurement interval of the assay, or at the lowest QC concentrations, should be used for the last SSS to evaluate the response of the instrument. The S/N ratio for the response must be at least 10:1. If multiplexed HPLC systems are used, acceptable SSS need to be documented on each system.
Generally, these samples should be made of standard or IS material in a suitable solvent at a known concentration near the middle of the analytical measurement interval or near any medical decision point(s), should they exist. Because the SSS is used to ensure proper analytical performance of the instrumentation, it is not necessary to process the sample (eg, extraction, protein crash), or to use a complex matrix.

chunks.text: It is important for the retention time to remain constant for accurate peak selection for analysis of samples. Retention time should be monitored for all peaks during analysis. An acceptable limit should be established during method verification; a tolerance should be specified in the SOP and should be used as part of a laboratory's QA assessment of results. The retention time for analyte and IS peaks should be similar to that of the standards. Additionally, the addition of a retention time standard of the pure analyte of interest may be included in the analysis to monitor any changes in retention time. It is recommended that the ratio of the chromatographic retention time of the analyte to that of the IS should correspond to that of the calibration solution at a tolerance of ± 2.5% for LC (see CLSI document C50 1 ). Retention times should be monitored both within and between runs to determine if trends are present. If a shift in retention time is observed, it could be a result of several factors, as described in Chapter 6.4.1.

chunks.text: Peak areas for the IS in calibrators and controls should be consistent within a run, having a %CV relative SD less than a predefined value for the method (eg, < 5% to 10%). Allowable total analytical error, bias, and precision may be defined for many analytes in terms of biological variation. 104 Failing this, allowable analytical error may be estimated from the precision and trueness necessary to maintain clinical utility. For therapeutic drug monitoring, a nonphysiological condition, allowable error can be estimated from pharmacokinetics. 105,106 Sources of error may vary by method, and these are not necessarily independent variables, but total error should be constrained such that the end result is useful. For chromatographic systems with multiple channels, peak areas should be consistent across channels. An acceptable range for IS peak area, with upper and lower limits, should be defined during method development. This can be defined as a minimum acceptable IS peak area, or a peak area range based on the variability of the method. Peak areas for the IS in individual samples may vary, reflecting differences in extraction and possibly competing interferences. Gross deviation evidenced by an outlier or by an overall increase in %CV is grounds for greater scrutiny of individual samples or the entire run. Given that calibrators and controls are prepared using pools, and then apportioned for individual use, IS values and ratios should show less variation than patient samples. IS areas should be comparable across calibrators and comparable for controls within run such that the contribution to TEa is not excessive. Greater variation may occur between runs, reflecting, for example, column usage and changes in system conditions. Gross variation for an individual sample may reflect double addition or contamination. The IS may show greater variation for analytical samples, depending on complexity of sample extraction and the presence of metabolites.

chunks.text:
Peak areas for the IS should be roughly consistent from run to run; however, this is less important than repeatable (within-run) consistency. A gradual decrease in peak area may reflect deterioration of the IS, quadrupole charging, a decrease in detector sensitivity, or a more general problem with the method or reagents. It is helpful to determine whether the change is restricted to the IS, or affects other analyte peaks as well, which may represent a more general problem. In method development, the IS concentration will have been chosen to yield a peak area somewhere in the middle of the analytical range, or close to a medical decision point. A predefined fraction of this value based upon the precision necessary to keep the allowable error within limits should be specified as the minimal acceptable area for the IS. This will not normally be close to the LLMI.
A minimal peak area for the lowest nonzero calibrator should be established during method development. A minimum S/N ratio for any reportable peak must be established by the analyst, but must be > 10, in particular at the LLMI. 49,55 The method should include criteria for exclusion of discrepant measurements, and for the number of calibrators needed for an acceptable run. Aberrant calibrators at the high or low ends of a calibration curve may be excluded, while results obtained within the remaining portion of the curve may be reportable if the remaining measurements are enough to establish a valid curve, as dictated by the method chosen for data reduction. Usually, this means a statistically significant change in confidence interval for the correlation coefficient, but the calculation will vary depending on weighting and whether the curve is linear, quadratic, and so on. This is an important consideration, as residuals are not independent (ie, they sum to zero). 107

chunks.text: Peak areas for calibrators should be relatively consistent between runs. Decreasing calibrator peak areas over successive runs may reflect calibrator deterioration. Comparison to the IS, control materials, and other repeated samples can help to clarify whether the problem is limited to calibrators or a more general problem with the method, reagents, or instrumentation. Deterioration limited to the calibrators is problematic, as it will result in proportionately spurious analytical results. Allowable bias should be < 5% to 10%. 37 Peak area ratios for each calibrator concentration to the IS should fall within defined limits and have CV < 6%. Total imprecision, within or between runs, must be ≤ 20% at the LLMI, and ≤ 15% over the rest of the measuring interval (see CLSI document QMS24 101 ). Better precision may be needed for specific analytes (see CLSI document QMS24 101 ).

The calibration slope for each analyte should be documented and monitored for deviation from an allowable interval. Acceptability criteria to define an allowable interval for the calibration slope should be established in advance and determined based on method verification studies. The acceptability criteria can be established by plotting all calibration data points from the method verification studies, which will provide an estimate of the variation expected for the calibration curve. Typically, these will be expressed as percent deviation from an expected value. Minimal criteria include total allowable bias ≤ 15% at all values above the LLMI, and r  ≥ 0.995. 2 37 More stringent criteria may be appropriate for certain analytes. In these situations, acceptability criteria can be based on biological variation, clinical guidelines established by expert groups, or regional regulatory requirements.
The monitoring of calibration slopes should be performed with each run and deemed acceptable within a predefined allowable error before patient results are reported. An acceptable slope for the calibration curve is necessary but not sufficient for an acceptable run. Other parameters such as QC results, retention time monitoring, and IS signal should be used in conjunction with calibration slope monitoring to determine the acceptability of each run. Progressive decline in slope may suggest calibrator deterioration or a loss of detector sensitivity.

As mentioned in Chapters 6.1 and 7.4, it is important to use ion ratios as an added layer of assay selectivity. The ion ratio for any given analyte or IS should not vary significantly within or between runs, and so should be used in every run to determine whether there may be an interference present in any of the patient samples. The acceptance criteria for ion ratios for each analyte should be determined during method development. The software from most mass spectrometer vendors is capable of calculating the ion ratios for the user, or, if necessary, the user can calculate the ion ratios using computer software (see Chapter 6.4.5). Patient results should be flagged if the ion ratio falls outside of acceptability criteria, as this may be indicative of an interference. This would require further review based upon medical decision points. Additionally, if the ion ratio is changing significantly between runs for the standards used to construct the calibration curve, this may be indicative of an ionization problem and should be investigated. If the quantifier ion peak area is sufficiently low (eg, around the LLMI of the assay) that the qualifier ion peak cannot be seen in a particular patient sample, this would require a higher level of review (eg, by a supervisor or laboratory director) relative to the medical decision point to determine if the result could be reported. However, in toxicology, where quantifier and qualifier ions are required for identification, patient results should not be reported in the absence of any ion.

Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) subscribes to a quality management system (QMS) approach in the development of standards and guidelines that facilitates project management, defines a document structure using a template, and provides a process to identify needed documents. The QMS approach applies a core set of 'quality system essentials' (QSEs), basic to any organization, to all operations in any health care service's path of workflow (ie, operational aspects that define how a particular product or service is provided). The QSEs provide the framework for delivery of any type of product or service, serving as a manager's guide. The QSEs are:
· Organization and Leadership
· Supplier and Inventory Management
· Information Management
· Customer Focus
· Facilities and Safety Management
· Equipment Management
· Process Management
· Nonconforming Event Management
· Assessments
· Personnel Management
· Documents and Records Management
· Continual Improvement
The QSEs covered by C62 and its related CLSI documents are available on the CLSI website: https:/ /clsi.org/qse

The analyte of interest is ionized in the source of the mass spectrometer by any of a variety of mechanisms (see Chapter 4.2). Once ionized, analyte ions travel to the mass analyzer component of the mass spectrometer, where ions are selected according to their mass-to-charge ratio ( m/z ). Ions produced from small molecule analytes (< 1000 Da) usually possess a single charge; therefore, their m/z is equivalent to the mass of the ion. This is commonly designated as [M + H] +  for protonated (positive) and [M - H]  for deprotonated (negative) ions. -The selected ions then travel to the detector where they are counted. The data output is presented as a mass spectrum, with the m/z plotted on the x-axis and the relative abundance of ions plotted on the y-axis. When coupled to an LC system, a chromatogram can be generated in which relative ion abundance of a specific m/z is plotted vs time (see CLSI document C50 1 ). 4.3.1 Quadrupole Mass Analyzers

In the literature, the term 'eicosanoids,' which chemically refers to species comprised of 20 carbons, was used generically to include related structures of fatty acids with different chain lengths ( 9,  10 ).  In  more  recent  years,  the  term  'oxylipin'  has  become  more  generally  used because it chemically includes all oxygenated metabolites of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and PUFAs regardless of chain length or synthetic origin ( 11 ). 1. Introduction.
As summarized in the accompanying Focus article, research on eicosanoids such as prostaglandins and related mediators originated during the 1930s, with seminal work by Kurzrock and Lieb ( 1 ), and von  Euler  ( 2 ), which  was  then  followed  by  the  structural  identification  and  characterization  of prostaglandins (PGs) and thromboxanes (TXs) by Bergström, Samuelsson and Hamberg in the 1960s and 1970s ( 3-5 ). During that time, related oxygenated structures were discovered, which originated from both longer- and shorter-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), such as docosahexaenoic and linoleic acids ( 6-8 ). In the literature, the term 'eicosanoids,' which chemically refers to species comprised of 20 carbons, was used generically to include related structures of fatty acids with different chain lengths ( 9,  10 ).  In  more  recent  years,  the  term  'oxylipin'  has  become  more  generally  used because it chemically includes all oxygenated metabolites of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and PUFAs regardless of chain length or synthetic origin ( 11 ). 'Oxylipin' will be used hereafter to refer to relevant species being analyzed with the targeted methods described herein.

chunks.text: The  sensitive  and  selective  analysis  of  oxylipins  and  their  downstream  metabolites  requires  the combination  of  chromatography  and  tandem  mass  spectrometry  (MS/MS),  with  many  studies describing targeted methods for their analysis in human plasma, serum, urine, and other biological samples over the last 50 years. With advances in liquid chromatography (LC) and the availability of sensitive MS/MS systems originating in the early 2000s, comprehensive chromatographic approaches to separating and quantifying up to and beyond 100 eicosanoids using pure chemical standards and appropriate internal standards were developed ( 9, 12-16 ). This analysis later expanded to include a more comprehensive set of oxylipins when instruments with increased sensitivity and functionality became available ( 17-26 ). A selection of papers from the field are cited here, along with more recent reviews for background information ( 13-16, 27-36 ). Additional studies describe the overall fragmentation behavior of oxylipins in the gas phase after collision-induced dissociation (CID) ( 37, 38 ). Although gas chromatography is well suited for the analysis of (derivatized) oxylipins, since the 2000s it has been superseded by LC combined with MS/MS, for which derivatization is not required. MS/MS interfaced  with  electrospray  ionization  (ESI),  operating  usually  in  negative  ion  mode,  detects  all species resulting from the deprotonation of the carboxyl group. Only a few oxylipins are sometimes monitored in positive ion mode, for example, leukotriene C  (LTC ), in which the glutamic acid amino 4 4 group is ionized ( 38 ).

chunks.text: Not all isomers of oxylipins are well separated by reversed-phase (RP) LC [for example, 12-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic  acid  (HETE)  and  8-HETE,  7,17-dihydroxydocosahexaenoic  acid  (DiHDoHE)  and 7,14-DiHDoHE)]. Therefore,  selective  MS  detection  is  undertaken  after  CID  to  form  characteristic fragments.  The  quantification  of  oxylipins  in  biological  samples  generally  requires  high-sensitivity assays because of their low abundance. However, some species have been reported at relatively high endogenous  concentrations  [for example,  9-hydroxyoctadecadienoic  acid  (HODE)],  and  thus monitoring diverse species may require methods that have a wide dynamic quantification range. Triple quadrupole  mass  analyzers,  operating  in  multiple-reaction  monitoring  (MRM)  mode,  also  called selected  reaction  monitoring  mode  (SRM),  are  most  often  used  for  quantitative  oxylipin  analysis. These recommendations focus on analytical (detection and quantitation of oxylipins by LC-MS/MS) and  post-analytical  (result  reporting  and  nomenclature)  aspects  of  the  measurement  process. Although the preanalytical pipeline is not covered in these recommendations, it may be useful to note that artefactual oxidation can occur during sample storage or preparation and this can lead to the formation of substantial amounts of several oxylipins ( 39, 40 ). In addition, the generation of serum from whole blood results in the activation of leukocyte and platelet enzymes that generate abundant oxylipins ( 41, 42 ).

chunks.text:
Over the last 20 years, interest in lipid analysis using MS (lipidomics) increased substantially with numerous methods for analyzing large numbers of these molecules being developed and applied. This rapid development of the research field led to inconsistent data, uncertainty about data reporting, and hence reproducibility  issues,  particularly  in  relation  to  the  use  of  untargeted  methods  ( 43-45 ).  To address this, community initiatives were established, which included the development of a 'minimal reporting list' for the field of lipidomics, as well as structured advice on how to annotate lipids based on the level of information provided by the analytical method, using shorthand nomenclature ( 46-49 ). Separately, but related to these new recommendations, in the oxylipin field, it became apparent that the detection of oxylipins called specialized pro-resolving mediators ( 50 ) may have, in some instances, not conformed to expected standards in the field, as discussed previously ( 51-55 ).
In the following paragraphs, methods and approaches to ensure robust and reproducible analysis of oxylipins using LC-MS/MS are presented, aiming to support the community with agreed principles to be applied in a discovery research setting. Measurements of specific oxylipins conducted as part of clinical studies (for example, trials for drugs or other interventions in humans) or patient diagnostics need to meet criteria outlined in international bioanalytical guidelines, in addition to this document ( 5658 ). Adopting analysis parameters described in the literature without method validation (parameters such as selectivity, sensitivity, calibration range, accuracy and precision as discussed later) is not recommended, because even on the same platform, instrument parameters can vary.
This  recommendation  is  structured  to  provide  guidance  to  researchers  for  both  (i)  initial  method development  and  (ii)  reporting  data  generated  by  established  methods.  In  the  case  of  method development, all parameters described in boxes as 'Method Development' can be reported, whereas if  using  an  established routine assay, studies can instead report parameters listed under 'Routine Analysis',  either  in  the  main  text  or  a  supplementary  section.  Any  deviations  from  the  reporting standards outlined here should be clearly reported. We also recommend that the Lipidomics Reporting Checklist is used as a template for reporting ( 46 ).

chunks.text: Because of the structural complexity of oxylipins, numerous isomers of individual species with the same general structure can exist. For example, there are at least 10 different positional isomers for HDoHE, all forming a precursor [M-H]  ion with the same -mz / value. Whereas the overall pattern of fragment  ions  is  distinct  for  each  oxylipin  structure,  individual  fragments  are  not  always  specific. Furthermore, oxylipins with related structures can give rise to the same precursor-product ion mz / transition pairs, that is, SRM/MRM transitions (fig. S1). This is of particular concern for isomers, such as  enantiomers,  diastereomers,  and  geometric  isomers.  Because  of  this  issue,  chromatographic separation is required for the selective detection and quantification of individual oxylipins. This is most often undertaken using (ultra)high-performance reversed-phase columns filled with  particles smaller than 2 µm or core-shell particles of 3 µm size, applying a gradient of acidified water and organic solvent mixtures of methanol, acetonitrile, and/or 2-propanol. Numerous methods are described that enable the efficient separation of oxylipins into narrow chromatographic peaks that are well retained on the column and cleanly resolved from isobars ( 16, 20, 21, 23, 32 ). These methods can be used to guide chromatographic  method  development  and  may  require  adjustments  depending  on  the  specific instrumentation and instrument configuration. In addition to RP separation, additional chromatographic systems, including normal-phase/chiral ( 13, 59 ), supercritical fluid chromatography ( 24, 60, 61 ), and capillary electrophoresis ( 62, 63 )  have been used for oxylipin analysis. These show an orthogonal chromatographic selectivity, which can be helpful for the characterization of oxylipins in biological samples.

During method development, it is important to determine isomeric oxylipins that share both precursor and product ions and elute closely, leading to overlap in retention times in the same MRM detection channel. Examples include: (i) PGE , PGD , and their 82 2 iso and 11-β isoforms, and (ii) LTB , 64 trans -LTB , and their C12 epimers, which elute within a narrow retention time window. Enzymatically formed 4 cis -epoxy-PUFAs elute close to, but slightly earlier than, trans -epoxy-PUFAs formed by nonenzymatic oxidation  using  RP  chromatography  and  generate  identical  MS/MS  spectra  ( 64 ). Furthermore, whereas epoxy- and hydroxy-PUFAs are detected with identical MRM transitions, they are generally well separated by chromatography (fig. S1). Additional examples of critical separation pairs are listed in table S1.
Uniquely among oxylipins, TXB  shows complex RP chromatographic behavior with a larger earlier 2 eluting peak followed by a smaller later peak, with both connected by a sloped line (fig. S2). In short chromatographic runs, or when present in very low amounts, TXB  can appear as a broad tailing peak. 2 This has been suggested to originate from tautomerism of the lactol ring ( 65 ); hence, it is advised to integrate the entire peak to generate a single value.

Image reproduced from Kampschulte et al . ( 39 ).

For example, 10( S ),17( S )-dihydroxy4( Z ),7( Z ),11( E ),13( Z ),15( E ),19( Z )-docosahexaenoic acid (PDX) and its enantiomer coelute and need to be separated from their related isomers for quantification (figs. If the full structure of the isomer is not confirmed, then only a partially annotated  name  (for  example,  10,17-DiHDoHE)  should  be  reported.  The  appropriate  naming  of oxylipins, based on the assay used, is discussed in more detail later.

To correctly identify and accurately quantify oxylipins, structurally meaningful oxylipin-specific MRM transitions need to be carefully selected, specifically the precursor [M-H]  ion and a product ion that is -at least in part specific for the molecule being analyzed. In the case of oxylipins, product ions are typically  formed  through  cleavage  of  a  C-C-bond  adjacent  to  an  oxygenated  functional  group  (αcleavage)  with  or  without  further fragmentation,  neutral  loss, or rearrangement.  Nonspecific fragmentation resulting from loss of CO /acetaldehyde [M-H-44]  or H O [M-H-18]  or multiples should 2 -2 -be avoided when more specific fragment ions are available, because distinguishing between CO  and ₂ acetaldehyde requires high-resolution MS.
When  establishing  an  assay,  method  parameters  described  in  publications  can  act  as  a  guide; however, instrument-specific optimization is still required. MS  source  parameters  (including temperature,  gas  flows,  and  ESI  voltage)  are  first  optimized  for  selected  representative  oxylipins. Parameters  specific  to  each  lipid,  such  as  collision  energy  (CE),  then  need  to  be  individually established  for  each  oxylipin  and  its  transitions.  Depending  on  the  instrument,  other  electronic parameters may then require optimization. Once MRM settings and chromatographic parameters are established, the simultaneous optimization of all targeted compound MS parameters can be performed ( 18 ).

When  selecting  product  ions  to  monitor  oxylipins,  it  is  important  to  consider  the  potential  for interference from co-eluting peaks in biological samples and which MRM transitions give the highest signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) both using standards and in extracted matrix samples. A secondary MRM transition (qualifier) can be monitored in addition to the quantifier ion to support the identification of an oxylipin. This is especially useful in the case of co-eluting isobars (analytes yielding ions with the same mz / )  when the particular oxylipin has not been previously shown to be present in the matrix being analyzed. A secondary MRM can also provide further evidence for functional group position (on which carbon the hydroxy or epoxy group is located). If an oxylipin bears more than one oxygen-containing functional group (hydroxy, epoxy, or keto group), an α-cleavage at each site is expected. For example, 7,17-DiHDoHE gives rise to fragment ions at mz / 140 and mz / 261 because of fragmentation at bonds on C7 and C17, respectively ( 21 ).  A  published  list  of  CID  fragments  from  over  180  oxylipins  and deuterated  internal  standard  can  aid  the  selection  of  transitions  for  metabolites  not  separated  by chromatography ( 19 ).
If two MRM transitions are monitored, the ratio of the quantifier to the qualifier (secondary) peak areas should be at a similar level (typically ± 30%) for the standard and the lipid in the sample, to evidence the structure. As an example, the MRM transition for 10,17-DiHDoHE shows several chromatographic peaks when analyzing biological samples (fig. S3). Whereas the ratio of the two transitions provides evidence for the presence of PDX in serum (fig. S4), the peak at the retention time of PD1 results from an isomer, another compound, or mixtures thereof ( 21, 39, 69 ). Here the quantifier/qualifier ratio clearly shows that the compound(s) detected in the targeted analysis of patient serum are not the same as the standard.

Fig. S4. A secondary MRM transition demonstrates the absence of PD1 and presence of PDX in serum. Oxylipins were extracted from healthy human serum spiked with PDX and PD1 (also known as NPD1) or from serum from patients with end-stage renal disease by solid-phase extraction. Chromatographic separation was performed on a 2.1×150 mm column with 1.8 µm fully porous RP18 particles using a gradient of water and acetonitrile/methanol. Oxylipins were detected on a 5500 QTRAP following ESI(-). Serum from healthy individuals did not yield signals of PDX or PD1. Left: Structures of PD1 and  PDX  as  previously  described  ( 70 ).  Middle:  Representative  peaks  from  standards  using  two  MRM transitions, m/z 359.1→153.1 and m/z 359.1→206.1, corresponding to the PDX and PD1 standards. Right: Area  ratios  of  the  oxylipin  reference  standards,  extracts  of  human  serum  spiked  with  the  reference standards (noting that serum from healthy subjects did not yield signals of either lipid), and extracts of serum from patients. Whereas the ion ratio is not affected by the matrix (standard vs. spiked healthy serum), differences between the patient serum and the standard are observed for the PD1 signal, indicating that it arises from a different oxylipin or a mixture of isomers that may or may not include an unknown amount of the lipid of interest. ( 21 69 , ).
Monitoring secondary MRMs and determining the ratio of qualifier and quantifier in a representative biological sample to demonstrate that it is consistent with that of the synthetic standard is important for low-abundant lipids, such as multiply oxygenated forms where many closely eluting or co-eluting isomers exist. However, for simultaneous quantification of large numbers of more abundant oxylipins, such as mono-hydroxy fatty acids (for example, 12-HETE) being measured in well-studied matrices, such as plasma, it is not routinely practical. This is due to limitations of the dwell and cycle times.

An alternative approach for establishing the structure involves the collection of a product-ion spectrum of the oxylipin in the sample at or around the apex of the chromatographic peak and comparing it to the spectrum of the standard obtained using the same method. If sufficient lipid is present, then triplequadrupole instruments can generate MS/MS spectra of sufficient quality for comparative purposes. QTRAP instruments, which can operate the third quadrupole as an ion trap, generate higher-quality spectra, particularly in cases where low amounts of the lipids are present. Here, the resulting spectra for  the  sample  and  standard  need  to  be  visually  comparable,  particularly  for  the  more  abundant structurally relevant ion m/z values, and their relative ratios (fig. S5). However, it is generally difficult to obtain spectra for comparison when analyzing very low amounts of lipids. In this situation, the use of qualifier and quantifier transitions and comparing their ratios (as discussed earlier) is more suitable for identity confirmation. Software tools for determining spectral fit are increasing in availability and popularity,  particularly  for  untargeted  and  discovery  studies  ( 71 ). However,  for  confirmation  of structure in targeted oxylipin assays, they should be used with caution and, in general, regardless of the result from a computational comparison, a strong clear visual match between the standard and the proposed biological compound is expected. The same major ions should be seen clear of the baseline in both standard and sample, and with similar relative ratios (fig. S5).
Fig.  S5.  Example  comparison  of  fragment  spectra  from  a  standard  and  a  cell-derived  oxylipin.
Tetranor 12-HETE was analyzed either from macrophage extracts (left) or a commercial standard (Cayman Chemical, right) using LC-MS/MS. Images reproduced from Misheva et al . with permission (72).

chunks.text:
For triple-quadrupole-based LC-MS/MS methods, the dwell time, which represents the duration of the detection of a single MRM transition, must be optimized in conjunction with the total cycle time for all transitions monitored. Short dwell times reduce the total cycle time and are useful when generating narrow chromatographic peaks, but they will also substantially reduce the sensitivity (based on S/N). On the other hand, if the cycle time is too long, S/N will be higher, but narrow peaks will not be defined properly when quantifying a large number of analytes, because there will be insufficient data points per peak.
For quantification, a minimum of 7 to 10, but ideally 20, data points per peak are required to define a peak ( 73 ). As an example, a typical chromatographic peak with a full width of 10 s would enable the measurement of only 50 transitions using a dwell time of 20 ms (cycle time 1 s; 1 Hz), while generating 10 points across the peak. If the detection of more transitions is desired, the MS method can be split into several periods as described previously ( 16 ), or, if the instrument allows it, scheduled MRM can be used. This is particularly important when using modern columns with sub-two micron particles.
With scheduling, the instrument only monitors each transition within a defined retention time window. This substantially reduces the number of MRM transitions being monitored at any particular time, enabling longer dwell times per analyte and thereby markedly improving data quality and sensitivity.
In scheduled mode, a fixed cycle time is defined, and dwell time is then dynamically adjusted based on the number of transitions being measured per individual cycle. The parameters for a scheduled MRM mode that need careful consideration, are as follows:
1. The cycle time should be sufficiently short to achieve the required number of data points per peak. A typical setting would be 0.5 s, which generates about 20 data points for a 10-s, full-width peak.
2. The detection window should be sufficiently wide to enable robust detection even if the retention time shifts and to enable recording of a full baseline on either side of the peak, enabling proper S/N calculations. Therefore, two to four full-peak widths should be monitored at both sides of the peak.

chunks.text:
Targeted quantification of oxylipins requires an authentic analytical standard of the target molecule. The use of the enantiomer of an authentic analytical standard, which co-elutes in RP chromatography, is also acceptable. Reliable quantification in complex biological samples also requires stable, isotopelabeled internal standards, which are usually added before extraction and sample preparation ( 13, 19 ). Quantification is then performed by external calibration, based on the ratio of analyte to the internal standard. Although not required for research assays, when the method is intended for clinical studies or patient diagnostics, external and internal standards should be certified with a guideline-conforming technique to determine absolute amounts (for example, q-NMR) ( 74 ).
Ideally, an isotopically labeled internal standard would be included for each oxylipin. Although these are not available for most oxylipins, it is encouraged to use as many as possible, with at least one for each group of structurally related analytes eluting at a similar retention time (for example, PGs, LTs, hydroxy-PUFAs, epoxy-PUFAs, and dihydroxy-PUFAs or multiple hydroxy-PUFAs). An isotopically labeled internal standard would ideally be included for a specific oxylipin when it is of greater interest to the study than others. This is because ion suppression caused by co-eluting molecules from the matrix can vary between the retention time of the internal standard and that of the analyte, and this would not be accurately corrected by the (analyte/ internal standard) area ratio. If ion suppression (see 'sample preparation' section below for detailed description of ion suppression analysis) is thought to specifically affect a subset of analytical targets in a sample matrix, a comparison of peak quantitation against  two  independent  internal  standards  (for  example, 2 H -5-HETE  and 4 2 H -15-HETE)  can  be 4 considered as a means of highlighting the issue. In addition, a representative extracted matrix pool can be used to generate a calibration curve dilution, and the slope of the analyte responses in the presence and absence of matrix can be compared. The stability and variation of the retention time of oxylipins in relation to their corresponding internal standard can also be evaluated to determine the relative retention time.

In addition, a representative extracted matrix pool can be used to generate a calibration curve dilution, and the slope of the analyte responses in the presence and absence of matrix can be compared. The stability and variation of the retention time of oxylipins in relation to their corresponding internal standard can also be evaluated to determine the relative retention time.

chunks.text: The  amount  of  internal  standard  to  add  should  be  informed  by  the  sensitivity  of  the  analysis. Specifically,  the  amount or concentration used should be within the lower range of the calibration standards  (for  example,  10  to  50  times  the  LLOQ).  However,  if  the  concentration  of  the  internal standard is too low, accurate integration may be difficult, particularly if losses or ion suppression occur. Conversely, if the internal standard amount is too high, a signal in the MRM trace of the unlabeled analyte  can  become  visible  because  of  inevitable  contamination  with  the  unlabeled  compound (generally < 1%), and/or it can cause ion suppression of the analyte. If a commercial external standard is not available, and the oxylipin structure is not fully defined, then analysts can report fold-changes relative to an internal standard instead of quantified amounts. This enables the generation of biological insight into the behavior of a given lipid, for example, upon treatment with a test compound. However, for naming such lipids, shorthand nomenclature, as described previously ( 47 )  is  more scientifically correct  than  full  stereochemical  names.  Furthermore,  the  data  would  be  reported  as  relative,  for example, percentage of control, and not quantitative. In this way, an oxylipin is only fully annotated when a synthetic reference standard is available.

The lowest amount on the column at which each oxylipin can individually be detected, as well as the lowest quantifiable amount, is determined separately for each oxylipin. These values are compoundspecific because of differences in ionization efficiency and fragmentation behavior. For a standard, this amount (in pmol or pg) is calculated based on the concentration of the standard in the solution and  the  injected  volume  (usually  5  to  20  µl).  Typically,  a  serial  dilution  of  primary  standards  is performed and measured several times. Therefore, the amount of oxylipin generating a S/N of at least 3.0 (for at least three repeated injections of primary standards) is first determined and set as the limit of detection (LOD) of the instrument.
The amount of standard injected that generates a S/N ≥ 5 is the lowest standard for which peaks are integrated and the starting point for the determination of the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ). The LLOQ of the instrument method is that (calibrator) level that also leads to an accuracy (calibrator recovery) of 100% ± 20% and a variation (CV) of ≤ 20% in repeated injections if tested.

To determine the S/N, the following parameters are considered:
∞ Unsmoothed chromatograms should be used to determine S/N.
∞ Chromatographic peaks should demonstrate visible stable baseline noise, ideally on both sides.
∞ S represents the height of the peak above the mean noise (N) of the baseline. For example, if the peak height is 6250 cps and the mean level noise is 875 cps (maximum: 1300; minimum: 450), then the peak signal is 5375 cps (fig. S6).
∞ N represents the absolute height of the noise (peak to valley; that is, the highest and the lowest point of the signal) determined across a representative period of the chromatogram, within the region of the scheduled MRM window usually covering at least one but ideally two peak widths.
∞ The noise in a blank injection (for example, methanol) can also be evaluated.
∞ The noise in an extraction blank injection should also be evaluated to ensure no interferences; for example, linoleic acid-derived HODEs are sometimes detected in extraction blanks.
∞ Care should be taken when software is used to determine S/N. It is important to note that some S/N calculation tools from instrument manufacturers generate incorrectly high S/N values, most likely because smoothing is applied and other parameters such as the SD of the noise are used in place of noise. If software is used, users should first determine that the software returns values that  are  consistent  with  simple  manual  calculation  as  described  earlier.  If  needed,  it  may  be possible to improve software performance by adjusting or correcting parameters, such as the noise  retention  time  window.  The  validation  of  any  software  used  and  its  settings  should  be reported in the manuscript.
∞ In  addition  to  S/N,  the  coefficient  of  variation  (%  CV)  or  relative  standard  deviation  (RSD)  of repeated  injections  can  be  used  to  inform  assay  sensitivity,  for  example,  ≤  20%  at  LLOQ. However, if this criterion is also reported, only analyte peaks in samples that have an S/N ≥ 5 should be considered for integration.

chunks.text:
∞ Alternative methods to determine S/N exist that are standard for clinical applications, including using the SD of the noise instead of noise ( 75 ) or doubling the signal height before dividing by noise  [2H/h,  where  H  is  the  height  of  the  peak  and  h  is  the  height  of  the  noise  (European Pharmacopoeia, Ph. Eur. ( 76 )]. This stringent level of validation requires the use of matrix-spiked standards ( 75 ) and is generally not feasible for the analysis of endogenous oxylipins in research settings  due  to  sample  number  and  volume  limitations.  If  researchers  decide  to  use  these approaches, it is essential to follow them fully, and some pointers are provided below.
1. Using the SD of baseline noise for h assumes that the noise is normally distributed and would result in a value for h that is approximately 20% of the peak-to-peak value (approx. 99% confidence interval). The minimum S/N required when using SD for noise must also be adjusted to be larger by a factor of 5.
2. Similarly,  if  2H/h  is  used,  the  resulting  S/N  values  for  the  LOQ  must  be  doubled  to compensate. For example, the LOQ for the Ph. Eur. ( 76 ) would become S/N ≥ 10, which is compatible with S/N ≥ 5, as suggested in these recommendations. If this is not corrected, poor-quality peaks may be processed.
3. The  LOQ  can  also  be  established  by  performing  precision  and  accuracy  studies  using repeated injections. Through this approach, the concentration that can be measured with a coefficient of variance (CV) <20% establishes the LOQ. For such studies, the experimental design  must  include  sufficient  samples  to  compute  the  CV  with  an  acceptable  95% confidence interval. When the CV of a low-concentration sample is used, the experimental design should be described, including sample count and other variance expected to be encountered (inter-assay, inter-day, inter-instrument).
Fig. S6. Representative illustration for the determination of S/N. The peak of the injection of a standard (0.25 nM, 0.4 pg on column) and signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio is determined.

chunks.text:
As  stated  earlier,  this  level  of  validation  is  generally  not  feasible  for  the  analysis  of  endogenous oxylipins in research settings because of the unavailability of analyte-free matrix, and low amounts of precious samples being available in many experiments. Other variance methods exist that use matrixmatched calibration curves, and these are also described for clinical studies and diagnostics, but they are also not usually feasible for research assays and are not covered in these recommendations.
Based on the criteria provided earlier, the LLOQ is defined for a given oxylipin and instrument as a unique amount ('pg or pmol on column' or concentration of the injected solution). For oxylipins, this is typically about 1 pg [see Table 2 in Schebb et al . ( 55 )] on column but can be as low as 0.1 pg on column for some lipids using the newest instruments ( 21, 24 ). Quantification of oxylipins in biological extracts can only be performed if the compound is present at this or greater amounts in the sample being  extracted.  The  LLOQ  can  instead  be  reported  as  the  minimal  amount  of  lipid  that  can  be quantified in a specific amount of biological sample (for example, a concentration in ng/ml or pg/mg tissue, from a defined volume or wet weight), provided that the corresponding signal in the instrument used fulfills the criteria described in this section.
It  is  important  to  note  that  the  presence  of  matrix  can  increase  the  LLOQ of an assay due to the detection  of  chemical  noise  generated  from  unrelated  components  present  in  the  sample  and  a reduced response to the analyte due to ion suppression. Because of this, an essential requirement for reliable  quantification  in  biological  samples  is  that  the  analyte  in  samples  demonstrates  a  clear chromatographic peak with a sufficient S/N of ≥ 5 for each reported value. Integrated area values alone, for  example, 2000 cps, cannot be used to determine the presence of a peak in a sample, because these amounts can also originate from background noise ( 51 ).

For the standard curve, starting from the LLOQ, a series of at least six concentrations of each oxylipin quantified is required for external calibration. At least two concentrations per order of magnitude (that I,  a  log-linear  distribution)  are  used.  For  example,  0.1,  0.3,  1,  3,  10,  30,  100,  300,  and  1000  nM, corresponding to 0.16, 0.48, 1.6, 4.8, 16, 48, 160, 480, and 1600 pg on column, respectively, with 5 µl injected for an oxylipin with the molecular weight 320 g/mol. Detailed procedures for preparing and analyzing a calibration series were published previously ( 18, 77-79 ). Standards of known purity such as those with a certificate are preferable, and laboratories are encouraged to confirm their purity and identity ( 80 ). Analysis of the calibration series should be performed in ascending order, starting with a solvent blank, and ending at the upper LOQ (ULOQ, top of linear range) or at the highest amount relevant for the samples being analyzed, followed by analysis of a solvent blank to evaluate injection carryover.  As  described  earlier,  it  is  advisable  that  the  concentrations  of  internal  standard  in  the standard curve and prepared samples being analyzed by LC-MS/MS are equivalent.
For calibration and calculation of the amount of lipid in the samples, the area of the oxylipin peak is divided by the area of the internal standard used. To improve the accuracy and efficiency of integration and peak-picking algorithms, peak-smoothing algorithms can be applied, but this should only be done after raw data peaks have been verified to exceed the minimum S/N criteria for LLOQ, as discussed earlier. A linear calibration function is generated by linear regression of the ratio of oxylipin and internal standard peak areas as a function of the oxylipin amount/concentration. Alternatively, the ratio of oxylipin  and  IS  amounts can be plotted on the x-axis. A reciprocal weighting of 1/x or 1/x  of the 2 analyte/I internal standard concentration/amount is strongly advised ( 81 ) because it leads to a better accuracy for quantification of low-abundant oxylipins.

The  calibrator  recovery  ['accuracy'  in  several  software  programs,  or  'relative  mean  error'  (RME) should be 100 ± 20% at LLOQ and 100 ± 15% for all other calibration points. The accuracy here describes  the  ratio  between  the  added  (actual)  concentration  of  the  compound  in  the  calibration solution and the concentration that is calculated using the regression function of the calibration series:
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->
In addition, the precision of the calculated amount of repeated injections (for example, n = 5 in three batches) can be evaluated and is expected to be in the range of <20% CV. The linear range of the method can also be defined, starting with the LLOQ, up to the upper limit of quantification (ULOQ), the greatest amount of standard that results in a linear detector response with an accuracy of 100 ± 15% for repeated injections.
In samples, amounts of oxylipins can only be determined if the amount detected is within the linear range. In research settings, limited amounts of matrix often constrain the generation of matrix-matched calibrations.  Thus,  the  method  of  matrix-free  external  calibration  with  internal  standard  described earlier is common practice. However, determining and reporting recovery (accuracy) and variation (precision) by standard additions (spiking to samples) is recommended as part of initial development and establishment of a method.
Direct  quantification  based  on  internal  standard  can  be  conducted  for  individual  oxylipins  if  their corresponding internal standard is available and the method is operating in the linear dynamic range, as described earlier. For this approach, it is essential to determine the response factors of the analytes relative to the internal standard.

chunks.text: Before LC-MS/MS, extraction of oxylipins from biological samples reduces the amounts of interfering molecules, such as proteins and concentrates analytes of interest, in an LC-MS-compatible solvent. This can be achieved by several methods, including protein precipitation ( 23 ), liquid/liquid extraction, solid phase extraction (SPE), or a combination thereof ( 82 ). Most often, SPE procedures are used because they also (at least partially) remove other highly abundant lipids, such as phospholipids and neutral  lipids.  Note  that  some  oxylipins  are  unstable  during  handling  and  extraction  (for  example prostaglandins  show  pH  sensitivity  and  instability  during  base  hydrolysis),  with  many  being  also present in complex lipid pools ( 19, 83 ). Thus, it is important to assess the stabilities of oxylipins and internal standards during sample processing, particularly for the determination of total (hydrolyzed) oxylipins. In addition, certain oxylipins can be formed during sample preparation (for example, the clotting process used to produce serum) and extraction if appropriate precautions are not taken ( 40, 77, 84 ).

8. Sample preparation and ion suppression analysis.
Before LC-MS/MS, extraction of oxylipins from biological samples reduces the amounts of interfering molecules, such as proteins and concentrates analytes of interest, in an LC-MS-compatible solvent. This can be achieved by several methods, including protein precipitation ( 23 ), liquid/liquid extraction, solid phase extraction (SPE), or a combination thereof ( 82 ). Most often, SPE procedures are used because they also (at least partially) remove other highly abundant lipids, such as phospholipids and neutral  lipids.  Note  that  some  oxylipins  are  unstable  during  handling  and  extraction  (for  example prostaglandins  show  pH  sensitivity  and  instability  during  base  hydrolysis),  with  many  being  also present in complex lipid pools ( 19, 83 ). Thus, it is important to assess the stabilities of oxylipins and internal standards during sample processing, particularly for the determination of total (hydrolyzed) oxylipins. In addition, certain oxylipins can be formed during sample preparation (for example, the clotting process used to produce serum) and extraction if appropriate precautions are not taken ( 40, 77, 84 ).

headings: 8. Sample preparation and ion suppression analysis.

chunks.text:
Co-extracted compounds from matrix can cause substantial ion suppression (or 'ion enhancement', both are referred to here as 'ion suppression') of oxylipins and their corresponding internal standards. To check this, during method development, the detection of internal standards in extracted samples can be monitored. Where apparent recovery of the internal standard appears low (< 50%), it can be determined whether this is caused by ion suppression, low extraction recovery, or degradation of the compound.  This  can  be  assessed  by  comparing  data  generated  from  a  sample  with  the  internal standard added at the beginning of sample preparation with a sample for which the internal standard was added at the end of sample preparation directly to the extract (fig. S7). If ion suppression dampens detection of the internal standard, the signal will be reduced in both samples. In this case, sample preparation and/or chromatographic conditions may require further optimization ( 82, 85 ), and it should be evaluated whether a different internal standard should be used instead. Note that ion suppression can markedly vary across the chromatogram, and consequently, between an internal standard and its associated analyte(s). As an example, ion suppression for linoleic acid-derived HODE is different from AA-derived HETE in plasma lipid extracts, because the oxylipins elute at different retention times ( 82 ). Ion suppression analysis (Fig. S7) can be applied to monitor these effects.

Alternatively, dilution integrity experiments can be performed. For this, the prepared solution ready for injection into the LC-MS is analyzed after a two- to ten-fold dilution, and the concentrations calculated based on the internal standard and external calibration are compared. If this is observed, measures to reduce ion suppression should be considered, including modifying the choice of is the internal standard.

8. Sample preparation and ion suppression analysis.
Co-extracted compounds from matrix can cause substantial ion suppression (or 'ion enhancement', both are referred to here as 'ion suppression') of oxylipins and their corresponding internal standards. To check this, during method development, the detection of internal standards in extracted samples can be monitored. Where apparent recovery of the internal standard appears low (< 50%), it can be determined whether this is caused by ion suppression, low extraction recovery, or degradation of the compound.  This  can  be  assessed  by  comparing  data  generated  from  a  sample  with  the  internal standard added at the beginning of sample preparation with a sample for which the internal standard was added at the end of sample preparation directly to the extract (fig. S7). If ion suppression dampens detection of the internal standard, the signal will be reduced in both samples. In this case, sample preparation and/or chromatographic conditions may require further optimization ( 82, 85 ), and it should be evaluated whether a different internal standard should be used instead. Note that ion suppression can markedly vary across the chromatogram, and consequently, between an internal standard and its associated analyte(s). As an example, ion suppression for linoleic acid-derived HODE is different from AA-derived HETE in plasma lipid extracts, because the oxylipins elute at different retention times ( 82 ). Ion suppression analysis (Fig. S7) can be applied to monitor these effects.

After correcting for dilution, the same concentration is expected for each dilution. Significantly higher or lower amounts of oxylipin after dilution  indicate that the signals of the analyte and the allocated internal standard are not equally interfered with by matrix effects. If this is observed, measures to reduce ion suppression should be considered, including modifying the choice of is the internal standard.

During method development, accuracy and precision should ideally be determined for each sample matrix of interest (for example, plasma or urine) to demonstrate the suitability of the method. However, it  is  recognized  that  in  research  settings,  analytical  laboratories  routinely  analyze  many  types  of samples, and sufficient biological material is often not available for this purpose. Therefore, accuracy and precision could at least be provided for a relevant matrix when the method is being established.
The performance of the method for the quantification of (representative) oxylipins can be evaluated by repeatedly analyzing spiked samples. If a matrix without the oxylipin of interest is available (which is rarely  the  case),  then  two  relevant  amounts  can  be  added  (one  close  to  the  LLOQ)  to  determine accuracy and precision. Alternatively, an extracted matrix pool can be used to generate a calibration curve dilution, and the slope of the analyte responses in the presence and absence of matrix can be compared. An example of the determination of accuracy and precision of multiple hydroxy-PUFA in plasma and serum is shown in table S2.

A challenge with oxylipin quantification is that most biological matrices contain oxylipins. To overcome this, a heavy isotope-labeled oxylipin may be used, or a non-labeled oxylipin standard can be added at different amounts. When the added amount is plotted against the analyte-to- internal standard ratio, the linear regression function is expected to be parallel to that of the calibration. For the latter, spiking amounts should be adjusted to be close to the amounts identified in the actual sample (for example, equal to and double that of the endogenous amount present).
By preparing and analyzing a set (n = three to six) of non-spiked and spiked samples over three days, intra-day and inter-day precision can be determined. With respect to precision over multiple days with the same sample, it is recommended to prepare different aliquots rather than thawing the same sample multiple times. The stability of extracted samples and maximum storage times between preparation and  analysis  in  the  freezer  and/or  in  the  autosampler  can  be  monitored  and  reported,  because extracted oxylipins can degrade rapidly or alternatively form ex vivo ( 39, 40, 77, 84, 86, 87 ). Related to this, oxylipin amounts in fluids and tissues can change during storage. This is especially important to consider when samples have been stored for several years. Numerous studies have investigated changes in the patterns of oxylipins after storage and the effect of pre-analytical procedures such as plasma generation from whole blood ( 30, 40, 77, 84, 86-88 ).  A  simple strategy to test for stability involves the addition of a 13 C-labeled internal standard at the time of collection and monitoring its loss alongside endogenous oxylipins in the sample.
It  is  recommended  to  include  at  least  one  quality  control  (QC)  sample,  containing,  if  possible,  all analytes in a batch, to monitor the performance and stability of the analytical workflow. This can be generated from a pooled, spiked, and aliquoted biofluid sample (as relevant), or from a larger pool of homogenized and aliquoted tissue or cell pellet samples. QC samples can be included in each batch at defined intervals, and the analyst is encouraged to define pass/fail criteria, for example, a deviation from expected concentration <30%.

Because solid tissues can be highly heterogeneous, it is important to use optimized homogenization and extraction methods that yield reproducible recoveries of internal standards and analytes. Because of  this,  attention  should  be  paid  to  potential  sources  of  variability  in internal  standard  response  in complex tissue samples. This also applies to more conventional fluids, such as plasma and serum, which can vary substantially due to underlying disease. Maintaining a record of peak intensity of the internal standard in each run can help provide an early indicator of unanticipated interferences, as well as alerting the analyst to variations in instrument performance. It is also important to monitor method performance over time. To this end, basic QC procedures should be established in each laboratory performing quantitative oxylipin analysis. By analyzing control charts, using, for example, Westgard rules  ( 89,  90 ),  analytical  accuracy  and  precision  can  be  monitored  and  warning  and  action  limits defined.
Before commencing a sample analysis, acceptable instrument performance should be demonstrated, both for chromatographic separation and MS sensitivity. It is suggested that a low-level or a mediumlevel standard (system suitability control, SSC) is injected for this purpose. If the complete calibration series is not run alongside each batch, selected calibration standards should be analyzed to validate that the entire calibration series is still valid. Injection of the full calibration series should be performed regularly, or with every batch, and always after instrument maintenance or repair.
